title: Lesson 8 - Guided Project: A Reusable Prompt Toolkit

content:
Every chart this course has built so far has used st.line_chart — quick, and genuinely fine for a fast look at a trend. This module starts by finding its real limit: st.bar_chart, st.line_chart, and st.area_chart all register as the identical vega_lite_chart element under AppTest, distinguishable only by parsing the real chart specification each one produces — no color control, no hover tooltip, no way to combine two encodings in one chart.
From there, the module builds the same visualizations with two purpose-built libraries — Plotly, for a real interactive bubble chart with hover and zoom; Altair, for the same data expressed as a declarative grammar of encodings — each confirmed against the actual figure object Streamlit hands back, not assumed correct from how it looks. A real choropleth map, built from the dataset&rsquo;s own iso_alpha country codes, closes out the toolkit before the guided project turns world_explorer.py into a genuine multi-chart dashboard.
Start with Lesson 1, …
summary: Streamlit's own bar_chart, line_chart, and area_chart all register under the same AppTest element type, distinguished only by parsing their real vega-lite spec -- the exact limit that motivates reaching for Plotly and Altair, both confirmed to genuinely change on interaction, …
title: Data Visualization in Streamlit

content:
Module 2 declared raw.trips as a source just far enough to prove ref() and source() build a dependency graph — one table, one line of YAML, nothing more. Production projects lean on sources for more than that: freshness checks that catch a loader silently failing days before anyone notices missing rows, a naming convention that makes a hundred staging models navigable at a glance, and a staging layer that covers every raw table a project has, not just the one a prior module happened to need.
This module treats all three as first-class subjects. dbt source freshness runs against CityFlow&rsquo;s raw.trips — first with a common mistake (a business timestamp mistaken for a load timestamp, correctly flagged as stale), then fixed with a load-timestamp column and tested through passing, warning, and failing states. dbt Labs&rsquo; current staging-layer naming convention, stg_&lt;source&gt;__&lt;entity&gt;, gets applied: Module 2&rsquo;s stg_trips gets renamed to match it, with every ref() …
summary: How dbt distinguishes a source from a model, source freshness checks that catch a loader that silently stopped running, the current staging-layer naming convention, and a guided project staging every raw CityFlow table that exists.
title: Sources and Staging Models

content:
Module 2 designed cityflow-trip-events — six partitions, keyed by pickup zone, with a written reason for every setting. This module writes to it. You&rsquo;ll construct a KafkaProducer and measure, directly, why a synchronous send costs roughly three times what an asynchronous one does, produce keyed trip events onto the real topic and confirm the routing holds at scale, then tune acks, batching, and compression with real before-and-after numbers instead of taking the tradeoffs on faith.
Two kinds of real producer failure show up here too, on purpose, and each is handled differently: one raises straight out of send() before a future even exists, the other slips past send() and only surfaces once the broker actually rejects the message. Confusing the two — or catching neither — is exactly how a real pipeline silently drops data, so this module builds both failure paths deliberately before the guided project puts everything together: a producer that reads actual January 2024 NYC taxi …
summary: Construct a real KafkaProducer, prove sync sends cost more than async ones, tune the configuration that actually moves throughput, handle a real failed send properly, and replay real CityFlow trip data onto Kafka as a paced event stream.
title: Producers: Writing Events to Kafka

content:
Module 1 pointed a query straight at a CSV file with no table in sight. Module 2 turned files into tables and built the SQL vocabulary to work with them. This module goes back to the files themselves and treats them as a first-class part of DuckDB&rsquo;s toolkit: the exact options that control how a CSV gets read, why Parquet is the format DuckDB reaches for by default, how to query a whole folder of files as if it were one table, when DuckDB&rsquo;s own schema detection needs a hand, and how to write query results back out to disk in either format.
None of this requires loading data into a database first. Every lesson in this module queries files directly, the same way Module 1 did — but with a much wider set of tools: explicit read_csv() options instead of relying entirely on auto-detection, COPY ... TO for writing Parquet and CSV, glob patterns for reading many files as one, and an explicit columns={} override for the one real case auto-detection can&rsquo;t solve on its own. The …
summary: Read CSV and Parquet files directly with DuckDB, control schema detection, glob many files at once, and export query results in either format.
title: Reading Files Directly — CSV, Parquet, and Many Files

content:
Modules 1 and 2 already used expressions constantly without naming them as their own thing — pl.col(&quot;category&quot;) == &quot;Kitchen&quot;, pl.when(...).then(...).otherwise(...), .is_null(). This module stops and looks directly at what an expression is: a portable description of a column transformation that isn&rsquo;t tied to any particular DataFrame until you hand it to .select(), .with_columns(), or .filter(). You&rsquo;ll see the exact same expression object run against two structurally different Thistlewood tables, proving that portability concretely rather than just asserting it.
From there, the module builds the vocabulary you&rsquo;ll use in every remaining module of this course: every shape of pl.col (a single column, several at once, a regex pattern, &ldquo;all columns,&rdquo; &ldquo;all but these&rdquo;), pl.lit for constant values, and derived columns built from Thistlewood arithmetic — a margin and margin percentage from the product catalog. You&rsquo;ll see the one …
summary: The core mental model of Polars: expressions as portable, reusable descriptions of a column transformation -- pl.col, select, with_columns, and filter.
title: Learn the Expression System Early

content:
Welcome to Authoring DAGs, Module 3 of Orchestrating Data Pipelines with Airflow. Module 2 proved the mechanics work: write a DAG, drop it in the folder, watch the scheduler pick it up and run it. This module goes deep on the writing half of that sentence — the real choices you make every time you author a DAG, and what each one actually changes about how Airflow runs your code.
You&rsquo;ll start by writing the exact same small computation two different ways — once with the TaskFlow API&rsquo;s @dag/@task decorators, once with classic PythonOperator instantiation and explicit &gt;&gt; — and prove, with a real file diff, that they produce identical output. From there you&rsquo;ll add BashOperator to the toolbox alongside PythonOperator, wire a DAG whose dependencies branch and reconverge (not just a straight line), and demonstrate all four ways Airflow lets you write a dependency: &gt;&gt;, &lt;&lt;, set_upstream, set_downstream. Then you&rsquo;ll make a task fail on purpose and watch …
summary: Go deep on how a DAG is actually written: the TaskFlow API against classic operators, PythonOperator vs BashOperator, real branching dependencies, and a real retry Airflow's own scheduler observes and recovers from.
title: Authoring DAGs

content:
Welcome to Building Images for Data Jobs, the third module of Docker &amp; Kubernetes for Data Engineering. Modules 1 and 2 taught you to run containers and to write a Dockerfile at all. This module is about writing a good one — the kind a data engineering team actually ships, where every choice has a measured reason instead of a guess.
You&rsquo;ll start by swapping one line in a working Dockerfile — python:3.13 for python:3.13-slim — and measuring exactly how many hundreds of megabytes that costs or saves. From there you&rsquo;ll hit a case the slim base alone can&rsquo;t solve: a dependency that needs a real C compiler to install, and a multi-stage build that lets you keep the compiler for the build and throw it away before you ship. You&rsquo;ll slim a bloated build context with .dockerignore and see, in real byte counts, why combining RUN instructions actually shrinks an image while splitting them doesn&rsquo;t. And you&rsquo;ll learn that &ldquo;did it work?&rdquo; means …
summary: Package a real Python data job into a slim, multi-stage image: measured size wins, a clean .dockerignore, and correct exit codes.
title: Building Images for Data Jobs

content:
Welcome to The Check — the module the whole course is built around. Everything before this was setup; everything after is application. The one sentence to carry from here on is this: a loop is only as good as its check. A loop attempts, checks, corrects, and repeats. If the check is weak, the loop confidently marches toward the wrong finish line and tells you it&rsquo;s done. Beginners pour all their energy into the prompt. The prompt is the cheap part. The check is the engineering.
In this module you&rsquo;ll learn to build checks that actually work. You&rsquo;ll see why the checker matters more than the prompt, and meet the main kinds of checks — from simple checklists to detailed rubrics, worked examples, hard tests, and real-world signals — and when each one fits. You&rsquo;ll learn to get honest grading out of an AI instead of the flattery it defaults to, using techniques like grading one thing at a time and giving the model permission to say &ldquo;I&rsquo;m not sure.&rdquo; …
summary: The core module. A loop is only as good as its check. Learn kinds of checks, honest self-review, splitting doer from reviewer, and catching a false 'done'.
title: The Check: How a Loop Knows It's Working

content:
Welcome to DataFrames &amp; Transformations, the third module — where you stop watching Spark and start driving it. The first two modules were about understanding: the ceiling that makes distributed engines necessary, and the machinery underneath Spark — lazy plans, RDDs, the DAG, lineage. You can now predict what Spark will do. This module makes you fluent enough to tell it what to do, correctly, on data that fights back. The DataFrame API is the tool you&rsquo;ll use every working day, and it rewards knowing it well: expressed cleanly, a transformation is something Catalyst can optimize; expressed carelessly, it&rsquo;s a shuffle you didn&rsquo;t need or a filter that quietly corrupts a total.
The through-line is CityFlow&rsquo;s real taxi quarter, and the data&rsquo;s genuine defects are the point rather than a distraction. You&rsquo;ll build derived columns — trip duration, fare-per-mile, pickup hour — with column expressions that are themselves lazy plan nodes. You&rsquo;ll filter …
summary: Stop watching Spark and start driving it. Master the DataFrame API on real data — columns and expressions, filtering and cleaning the taxi dataset's genuine dirt, joining the zone dimension with a broadcast, and grouping and aggregating — then rebuild the previous course's entire …
title: DataFrames & Transformations

content:
Welcome to Pandas at Scale, the third module — where the reduction plan you wrote in Module 1 becomes real, working code. Pandas is where most data engineers actually live, and a few habits are the difference between a DataFrame that fits comfortably and one that crashes your kernel.
You&rsquo;ll learn to downcast numeric columns to the smallest safe type, convert low-cardinality columns like payment type and zone to categoricals (often a huge saving), transform data without triggering the silent copies that double your memory, and write group-by aggregations that stay fast on millions of rows. The module closes with a guided project that packages everything into a reusable load_taxi() function — and measures the real memory it saves versus a naive load.
Start with Lesson 1, where a single downcast call quietly halves a column.
summary: Make pandas lean and fast: downcast numeric columns, use categoricals for low-cardinality data, avoid needless copies, and aggregate efficiently — executing Module 1's reduction plan on the real NYC taxi data to cut its memory by more than half.
title: Pandas at Scale

content:
Welcome to Multi-Head Attention, the third module. A single attention head, however well trained, can only express one attention pattern per position — one notion of what to look for. Real transformers run several heads at once, each free to attend to a different kind of relationship, and then combine what they find. This module builds that from scratch.
You&rsquo;ll start with the motivation: why one head isn&rsquo;t enough, shown with two heads that learn to attend to genuinely different things. Then you&rsquo;ll implement the mechanics — splitting the model dimension C C into h h heads of size C/h C/h , running scaled dot-product attention in parallel across all of them, and concatenating the results before a final output projection mixes them back together. Finally you&rsquo;ll derive the backward pass through the split, the concatenation, and the projection — reusing the single-head gradients from Module 2 — and verify it against numerical gradients. The guided project assembles a …
summary: One attention head learns one kind of relationship; a transformer runs many in parallel. Learn why multiple heads help, how to split the model dimension into heads, run them in parallel and concatenate, and backprop through the whole thing — building a gradient-checked multi-head …
title: Multi-Head Attention

content:
Welcome to Deterministic &amp; Reference Metrics, the third module. When a test case comes with a reference answer, you don&rsquo;t need a model or a human to score it — you can measure quality with plain code that runs in milliseconds and gives the same number every time. These metrics are the fast, cheap, reproducible backbone of any eval suite, and knowing their limits is as important as knowing how to compute them.
You&rsquo;ll start with exact match and the normalization that makes it fair, add token-level F1 so a mostly-right answer earns partial credit, then meet ROUGE and BLEU for longer generated text — and see clearly where each metric is trustworthy and where it quietly misleads for question answering. You&rsquo;ll also learn to check structured outputs against a schema, so a Docent answer that&rsquo;s supposed to be JSON with an answer and a doc_id actually is. The module ends with a guided project that assembles these into a real reference-metric scorecard for Docent. …
summary: When you have a reference answer, you can measure quality with code instead of judgement. Learn exact match and normalization, token-level F1, ROUGE and BLEU, and structured-output checks — then build a reference-metric scorecard for Docent.
title: Deterministic & Reference Metrics

content:
Welcome to Training Robust Models, the third module of the course. Knowing XGBoost&rsquo;s knobs is not the same as training a model you can trust. Real datasets are imbalanced, have missing values, and mix numbers with categories — and this module teaches you to handle all of it with confidence.
You&rsquo;ll use early stopping so you never have to guess how many trees to grow, and cross-validation with xgb.cv for honest performance estimates that do not depend on one lucky split. You&rsquo;ll learn why accuracy lies on imbalanced data and how scale_pos_weight and the right evaluation metrics fix it, and you&rsquo;ll see how XGBoost handles missing values and categorical features natively — no manual imputation or one-hot encoding required. A guided project closes the module by combining all of these into one robust training pipeline.
Every model here is trained for real, mostly on the Adult Income dataset with its genuine class imbalance and categorical columns. Start with Lesson 1, …
summary: Train XGBoost reliably on real, messy data: early stopping, cross-validation with xgb.cv, class imbalance, and native handling of missing values and categorical features.
title: Training Robust Models

content:
Welcome to Writing Quality, Tested Code, the third module of the Software Engineering Fundamentals course. Good architecture from Module 2 only pays off if the code inside it stays readable and correct as it changes. You&rsquo;ll start with clean code: naming, function size, and error handling, turning a tangled invoice-total function from Ledgerly into five small, well-named pieces.
From there, you&rsquo;ll build a real automated safety net. You&rsquo;ll learn the testing pyramid, write unit tests with test doubles instead of hitting a real payment gateway, and see what test coverage does and doesn&rsquo;t guarantee. The module then adds behaviour-driven development: writing scenarios in a shared language business and engineering both understand, and the Gherkin syntax — Feature, Scenario, Background, Scenario Outline — that makes those scenarios executable. A guided project closes the module by cleaning, testing, and specifying a real subscription-pause feature end to end.
Every test …
summary: Clean code practices, the testing pyramid, behaviour-driven development, and the Gherkin language, all verified for real against Ledgerly, a small invoicing app.
title: Writing Quality, Tested Code

content:
Welcome to Stationarity and Differencing, the third module of the course. Module 2 (Components and Decomposition) split Cyclepath into trend, seasonality, and residual and interpreted each one. But a series with a trend and a repeating seasonal wave is, by definition, not stationary: its mean keeps climbing and its typical value keeps swinging with the calendar. A stationary series is one whose statistical properties, like the mean, do not change over time. The ARIMA family of models you will meet starting in Module 5 (AR, MA, ARMA, ARIMA) assumes stationarity going in. That makes this module the bridge between &ldquo;I understand my series&rdquo; and &ldquo;I can actually model it&rdquo;.
You will start with what stationarity means precisely: constant mean, constant variance, and autocorrelation that does not depend on when you measure it. You will see informally that Cyclepath fails all three. Then you will make that judgment formal with the Augmented Dickey-Fuller test, a …
summary: Test whether a series is stationary with the Augmented Dickey-Fuller test, and learn to fix it when it isn't — trend differencing, seasonal differencing, and when a transformation actually helps.
title: Stationarity and Differencing

content:
Welcome to Power and Sample Size, the third module. You designed an experiment in Module 2 and set a minimum detectable effect — the smallest change worth catching. Now comes the question that decides whether the experiment can work at all: how many users do you need? Run too few and the test is underpowered — even a real, valuable effect will hide in the noise, and you&rsquo;ll wrongly conclude &ldquo;no difference.&rdquo; Run far too many and you&rsquo;ve wasted traffic and time you could have spent on the next test. Getting the size right, before you run, is what this module teaches.
You&rsquo;ll start with the two ways an experiment can be wrong: a Type I error (calling a difference real when it&rsquo;s just noise) and a Type II error (missing a real effect). You&rsquo;ll learn what statistical power is — the probability of detecting a true effect — and the four levers that control it. You&rsquo;ll compute the sample size a two-proportion test needs from your baseline, target …
summary: Decide how big your experiment needs to be before you run it — the two kinds of error, statistical power, and the formula (and simulation) that turn a target effect into a required sample size.
title: Power and Sample Size

content:
Welcome to Designing Tools, the third module. You can already build the agent loop — but a loop is only as good as the tools you give it. In practice, most of an agent&rsquo;s reliability comes down to tool design: whether Claude reaches for the right tool, fills in the arguments correctly, and recovers when something goes wrong. This module is about getting that right.
You&rsquo;ll learn what makes a tool Claude uses well — names, descriptions, and schemas that guide the model toward correct calls. You&rsquo;ll validate inputs with Pydantic, so a wrong argument is caught before it reaches your code (and you&rsquo;ll generate the tool&rsquo;s schema straight from the model). You&rsquo;ll build the error-and-repair loop, where a failed call comes back to Claude as a tool_result it can learn from and fix on the next step. And you&rsquo;ll cover the design patterns — tool granularity, parallel calls, side effects, and clear return values — that keep tool use dependable. The module ends by …
summary: Make tools Claude uses well and that fail safely — clear schemas, Pydantic validation, an error-and-repair loop, and the patterns that keep tool use reliable.
title: Designing Tools

content:
Welcome to Branching and Merging, the third module of the course — and the part of Git that makes real, parallel work possible. A branch lets you develop a feature, try an experiment, or fix a bug in isolation, without disturbing your main line of work. Merging brings those lines back together. Once branches click, you&rsquo;ll use them constantly — for every feature, every fix, every &ldquo;let me just try something.&rdquo;
You&rsquo;ll learn that a branch is simply a movable pointer to a commit, create and switch between branches with git switch and git branch, and understand the two ways Git merges — fast-forward and three-way. You&rsquo;ll face merge conflicts head-on, learn to read the conflict markers, and resolve them without fear. And you&rsquo;ll meet git stash, the command that shelves half-finished work so you can switch contexts in a hurry. The module ends with a guided project: you&rsquo;ll develop two features of SkyLog on separate branches and merge them both — including …
summary: Work on multiple things at once with branches, combine them with merges, resolve conflicts confidently, and shelve work in progress with stash.
title: Branching and Merging

content:
Welcome to Combining Tables with Joins — the module where your SQL stops living inside a single table and starts answering the questions that real databases are actually built to answer. Up to now you have queried one table at a time. But production databases almost never keep everything in one place. Customer details sit in one table, their purchases in another, the tracks they bought in a third. To turn that into a useful report, you have to bring the pieces back together.
Data for this module
Database: chinook.db — a digital music store (SQLite).
Open it in any SQLite client — DB Browser for SQLite, the sqlite3 CLI, or Python&rsquo;s sqlite3. Each lesson lists the specific tables it uses.
Throughout this module you will work with the Chinook database, a realistic model of a digital music store with tables for customers, invoices, tracks, albums, artists, employees, and more. Your job is to connect these tables the way a working analyst does: list every customer&rsquo;s purchases, …
summary: Bring data spread across many tables back together with inner, outer, self, and cross joins, plus set operators.
title: Combining Tables with Joins

content:
Welcome to HTTP Done Right, the third module of the course. Your Task Manager already reads and creates tasks — but a real API does more than return data: it communicates clearly. It says &ldquo;201 Created&rdquo; when something is made, &ldquo;404 Not Found&rdquo; when it isn&rsquo;t there, and &ldquo;422&rdquo; when input is invalid. It accepts more than JSON, too — login forms, request headers, cookies, and uploaded files. This module is about making your API a well-behaved member of the web.
You&rsquo;ll learn to return the right status codes and choose response types beyond JSON, raise clean errors with HTTPException and write custom exception handlers for your own error cases, and read headers, cookies, and form data. Then you&rsquo;ll handle file uploads — accepting a file, reading its contents, and reporting on it. The module ends with a guided project that hardens the Task Manager&rsquo;s endpoints with proper status codes, real error handling, and a file attachment.
Every …
summary: Speak HTTP fluently — return the right status codes and response types, handle errors cleanly, and accept headers, cookies, form data, and file uploads.
title: HTTP Done Right: Status, Errors, Forms & Files

content:
So far you have described data that already exists. Probability flips the question around: given what you know, how likely is something that hasn&rsquo;t happened yet? It is the mathematics of uncertainty, and it is the bridge between the descriptive statistics you have learned and the inference you will reach at the end of this course. Every confidence interval, every p-value, every machine-learning model that outputs a &ldquo;70% chance&rdquo; rests on the ideas in this module.
You will start by learning the two ways to pin a number on chance — estimating from data (relative frequency) and calculating from theory (equally likely outcomes) — and watch them converge as samples grow. Then you will learn the rules that let you combine events: the addition rule for &ldquo;or,&rdquo; the multiplication rule for &ldquo;and,&rdquo; complements for &ldquo;at least one,&rdquo; and the crucial idea of independence. You will finish with permutations and combinations, the counting tools that make …
summary: Learn to quantify uncertainty — estimating probabilities, the rules of probability, solving multi-step problems, and counting with permutations and combinations.
title: Probability Fundamentals

content:
Welcome to Tool Use &amp; Function Calling, the third module of the Generative AI &amp; LLM Engineering course. So far your model can only do one thing: produce text. It cannot look up today&rsquo;s weather, query your database, send an email, or even reliably multiply two large numbers. Tool use removes that ceiling. You give the model a set of functions it is allowed to call, and it decides when to call them — turning a chatbot into something that can actually act.
You&rsquo;ll start with why tools matter and watch the model honestly admit it can&rsquo;t fetch live data, then ask for a tool instead. You&rsquo;ll learn to define a tool with a JSON input schema, run the tool-use loop (the model requests a call, your code executes it, you return the result, the model continues) both by hand and with the SDK&rsquo;s tool runner, and handle the real-world cases: parallel tool calls, errors, and strict schemas that guarantee valid arguments. The capstone assembles several tools into a …
summary: Give a language model real tools — define functions it can call, run the tool-use loop, handle parallel calls and errors, and build a multi-tool workflow.
title: Tool Use & Function Calling

content:
Ready to master advanced Python programming? This module transforms intermediate Python users into professional developers capable of writing elegant, efficient, and maintainable code for complex data analytics projects.
Python Advanced builds directly on Python Basics, introducing powerful programming paradigms and industry-standard practices used by professional developers and data scientists worldwide.

content:
Welcome to Querying a CSV Without Loading It Module 1 wrote FROM 'thistlewood_orders_flat.csv' and DuckDB read it, inferring every column&rsquo;s type on its own. That default behavior gets you a long way, but it&rsquo;s making decisions for you — which delimiter the file uses, where the real data starts, which columns matter. This lesson takes those decisions back: the same read_csv() function, with the options that give you explicit control over how a file gets parsed, for the cases where a file doesn&rsquo;t look exactly like thistlewood_orders_flat.csv did.

content:
Welcome to What Is an Expression? Module 1&rsquo;s very first lesson already showed you an expression — pl.when(pl.col(&quot;category&quot;) == &quot;Kitchen&quot;).then(pl.col(&quot;unit_price&quot;) * 1.10).otherwise(pl.col(&quot;unit_price&quot;)) — without stopping to name what kind of object that is. content:

content:
Welcome to The Checker Matters More Than the Prompt This is the first lesson of the module the whole course points at, so let&rsquo;s open with its most important and most counterintuitive claim: the quality of a loop comes from the check, not the prompt. Almost everyone believes the opposite. When an AI gives us something wrong, our instinct is to rewrite the request — a better prompt, a cleverer instruction, a magic phrase. This lesson argues that instinct is misplaced, and that the effort you&rsquo;d spend perfecting prompts pays off far more when spent on the check.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Explain why the check, not the prompt, decides a loop&rsquo;s quality Describe the &ldquo;leverage&rdquo; difference between the prompt and the check Recognize the instinct to fix the prompt when the check is the real problem See why this module is the heart of the whole course Let&rsquo;s start with the instinct almost everyone has.
The Instinct to Blame the Prompt You …

title: Lesson 1 - The Checker Matters More Than the Prompt

content:
Welcome to Columns &amp; Expressions Module 2 taught you how Spark thinks — plans, lazy evaluation, the DAG — by watching it defer work you had described. You could predict its behaviour, but you were still narrating from the sidelines. This module puts the keys in your hands: the DataFrame API is the tool CityFlow&rsquo;s engineers reach for every working day, and it starts with the smallest unit of it — the column. Every filter you&rsquo;ll write in Lesson 2, every join key in Lesson 3, every aggregation in Lesson 4, and the whole zone-hour report in Lesson 5 is built from column expressions. Get this one idea right and the rest of the module is composition.
And there is one idea to get right, because it trips up every engineer arriving from pandas. In pandas, df[&quot;total_amount&quot;] hands you a Series — an actual array of 9.5 million numbers sitting in memory, which you can index, mutate, and print. In Spark, df[&quot;total_amount&quot;] hands you something that contains no …
summary: Learn the Spark Column as an expression, not a list of values, and build real derived columns on 9.5M taxi trips — trip duration (19.8 min on the first trip), fare-per-mile ($13.20), and pickup hour — while defusing the timestamp_ntz cast trap that silently makes a duration …
title: Lesson 1 - Columns & Expressions

content:
Welcome to Downcasting Numerics In Module 1 you profiled CityFlow&rsquo;s taxi sample and wrote a reduction plan. The plan was specific: the zone IDs and payment codes are stored as int64 (8 bytes each) but NYC has only 265 taxi zones and a handful of payment types, so they are overpaying 4–8×; the fare and distance columns are float64 (8 bytes each) but carry only a couple of decimal places, so float32 would halve them. This lesson executes the first line of that plan. Downcasting means replacing a column&rsquo;s dtype with the smallest numeric type that still holds its actual values, and pandas gives you two tools to do it precisely.
The stakes are the same ones Module 1 measured: the full month of trips expands from a 50 MB file to over 400 MB in pandas, and a big slice of that is numeric columns wearing a size they do not need. Narrowing them is the cheapest, safest memory win available — lossless for integers, and for floats bounded by a tolerance pandas checks for you. By the end …
summary: Shrink pandas int64/float64 columns to the smallest type that safely holds their real values with pd.to_numeric downcast and astype, then measure the exact memory saved on the NYC taxi sample.
title: Lesson 1 - Downcasting Numerics

content:
Welcome to Why One Head Isn&rsquo;t Enough In Module 2 you built a single self-attention head from scratch: you projected the input into queries, keys, and values, scored every query against every key, softmaxed the scores into weights, and mixed the values. That one head is the engine of the tiny GPT you are assembling. But there is a quiet limitation hiding inside it, and this module exists to fix it.
A single head has exactly one set of projection matrices, Wq, Wk, and Wv. Those three matrices decide, once and for all, what counts as &ldquo;relevant.&rdquo; So for any query position, the head produces a single attention distribution, one row of weights that sums to 1. It has one opinion about where to look. If a language needs to track both the word right before the current one and a matching word far back in the sentence, a lone head cannot do both at once. It has to pick.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Explain why a single attention head can express only one …
summary: See why a single attention head can only express one relationship per position, and run two independent heads in NumPy to prove they attend to genuinely different things.
title: Lesson 1 - Why One Head Isn't Enough

content:
Welcome to Exact Match &amp; Normalization In Module 2 you built and audited a golden set for Docent &ndash; our assistant for the Meridian serverless database docs &ndash; so now every question comes paired with a known-correct reference answer. This module turns those labels into scores you can compute with plain code: no model in the loop, no human grading, the same number every run. We start with the simplest metric of all, the one every other reference metric is measured against: exact match.
Exact match asks one question &ndash; does the model&rsquo;s output equal the reference? &ndash; and answers it with ==. That&rsquo;s the whole metric. It&rsquo;s perfectly reproducible, costs nothing, and needs no judgement. But raw string equality is also brutally literal: it thinks &quot;HTTP 429.&quot; and &quot;429&quot; are two different answers, even though any Meridian user would call them the same. The fix isn&rsquo;t to abandon exact match; it&rsquo;s to normalize both strings first …
summary: Learn exact match, the simplest reference metric, and the SQuAD-style normalization that keeps it from failing correct Docent answers over trivial formatting.
title: Lesson 1 - Exact Match & Normalization

Welcome to Clean Code and Best Practices In Module 2, you gave Ledgerly&rsquo;s codebase a solid shape: classes with clear boundaries, interfaces that hide their implementation, and designs that follow the SOLID principles. Good structure is not enough on its own. Inside a well-designed class, a single function can still be a mess of cryptic names and tangled logic that nobody on the team wants to touch.
This lesson opens Module 3, &ldquo;Writing Quality, Tested Code,&rdquo; where the focus shifts from how classes relate to each other, down to how individual lines of code read. You will take a real Ledgerly function that calculates an invoice total, one that mixes subtotal math, tier discounts, loyalty discounts, tax, and late fees into a single block with names like x, tmp, flag, and r. You will rewrite it step by step into small functions with names that explain themselves.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Rename variables and functions so their purpose is clear …
summary: Learn to write clean code through Ledgerly's invoice calculator — meaningful names, small single-purpose functions, honest comments, consistent formatting, and fail-fast error handling.
title: Lesson 1 - Clean Code and Best Practices

content:
Welcome to Early Stopping and Evaluation Sets Welcome to Module 3. In Module 2 you learned what XGBoost is and turned its main knobs by hand: n_estimators, learning_rate, max_depth, and the regularization terms. You saw how sensitive the model is to how many trees you grow. Too few and it underfits; too many and it slowly memorizes the training set. But you were still doing the one thing this module exists to stop: guessing a good value for n_estimators and hoping.
Our running team, Northwind Analytics, felt this directly. Their California Housing model kept improving as they added trees, so they kept raising n_estimators, retraining from scratch each time to check whether the extra trees still helped. That is slow, wasteful, and easy to get wrong. This module is about training models that are robust without that manual fiddling, and the first tool is the most useful one you will meet all module: early stopping. Instead of picking a tree count, you set a large cap, show XGBoost a …
summary: Let a held-out validation set choose the number of trees for you: configure early stopping on XGBoost, watch it stop before the 2000-tree cap on real California Housing data, and read back the best iteration.
title: Lesson 1 - Early Stopping and Evaluation Sets

content:
Welcome to What Is Stationarity? Module 2 (Components and Decomposition) ended by splitting Cyclepath into a rising trend and a repeating seasonal wave. That was useful for understanding the series. It also quietly proved something important: a series whose average keeps climbing and whose typical value swings with the calendar cannot be stationary. A stationary series is one whose statistical properties, like the mean, do not change over time. That word gets used constantly in forecasting, and for good reason. The ARIMA family of models this course builds toward, starting in Module 5 (AR, MA, ARMA, ARIMA), assumes that the series it is fitting is stationary. Before you fix that, which is this module&rsquo;s job, you need a precise definition of what &ldquo;stationary&rdquo; actually requires.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
State the three properties a stationary series must have: constant mean, constant variance, time-independent autocovariance Explain why …
summary: A stationary series has a mean, variance, and autocorrelation that don't depend on when you measure them. Cyclepath fails this on sight — its mean climbs 38% from the first half of the series to the second.
title: Lesson 1 - What Is Stationarity?

content:
Welcome to Significance and the Two Errors An experiment ends in a decision: ship the change, or don&rsquo;t. Like any yes/no call made under uncertainty, it can be wrong in two different ways — and they&rsquo;re not symmetric. You can see a difference that isn&rsquo;t really there and ship a change that does nothing. Or you can miss a difference that is there and kill a change that would have helped. Sizing an experiment is fundamentally about controlling how often each of those mistakes happens, so before we can compute a sample size, we need to name the two errors precisely and see what the &ldquo;significance level&rdquo; you&rsquo;ve heard about actually controls. That&rsquo;s this lesson.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Distinguish a Type I error (false positive) from a Type II error (false negative) Explain what the significance level α controls and what β is Read the decision matrix that relates the truth to your call See, in simulation, that a p&lt;0.05 …
summary: Every experiment can be wrong two ways: calling noise a real effect (Type I) or missing a real effect (Type II). See what the significance level really controls — and watch a p<0.05 test cry wolf 5% of the time in simulation.
title: Lesson 1 - Significance and the Two Errors

content:
Welcome to What Makes a Good Tool Here&rsquo;s a truth that surprises people: when an agent misbehaves, the culprit is usually not the model and not the loop — it&rsquo;s the tools. Claude calls the wrong tool because two descriptions sound alike. It passes a bad argument because the schema didn&rsquo;t constrain it. It produces a confusing answer because a tool returned a wall of unstructured text. The good news is that all of these are design problems you control. This lesson covers the four levers that make a tool Claude reaches for correctly and calls right the first time — the foundation for the validation and repair you&rsquo;ll add in the rest of the module.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Name tools clearly so Claude can tell them apart Write descriptions that say when to use a tool, not just what it does Constrain inputs with a tight, typed schema Return results that are easy for the model to use This builds on the tool definitions from Module 2. Let&rsquo;s …
summary: Design tools Claude reliably picks and calls correctly — clear verb-noun names, descriptions that say when to use them, tight input schemas, and clear return values.
title: Lesson 1 - What Makes a Good Tool

content:
Welcome to Branches Explained Up to now, SkyLog has had a single line of history: one commit after another on main. But real work isn&rsquo;t that tidy. You want to build a feature without breaking the working version, try an idea you might throw away, or fix a bug while another change is half-done. Branches make all of that safe. A branch is a separate line of development you can switch to, commit on, and later merge back — and the surprising part is how lightweight it is. In Git, a branch is nothing more than a movable pointer to a commit. Understanding that one idea makes branching feel simple instead of scary.
We&rsquo;ll keep using the SkyLog repository.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Explain what a Git branch actually is List branches with git branch and read the current-branch marker Create and switch branches with git switch See how commits move a branch and how branches diverge Let&rsquo;s begin.
What a Branch Really Is Here&rsquo;s the mental model that makes …
summary: Understand what a Git branch really is — a movable pointer to a commit — and learn to create, list, switch, and diverge branches without disturbing your main work.
title: Lesson 1 - Branches Explained

content:
Welcome to Estimating Probabilities Every time you check a weather app, read a poll, or trust a model that says &ldquo;70% likely,&rdquo; you are reading a probability — a single number that measures how likely something is. Before you can combine probabilities or reason about uncertainty, you need to answer a more basic question: where does that number come from in the first place?
There are two answers. Sometimes you count what actually happened in data, and sometimes you reason about what could happen from the structure of the problem. In this lesson you will do both — estimating a real probability from a dataset of penguins, calculating exact probabilities for coins and dice, and then running a simulation that shows the two ideas are really one.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Define a probability as a number between 0 and 1 and read it correctly Estimate an empirical probability from observed data as a relative frequency Calculate a theoretical probability when …
summary: Learn what a probability is, how to estimate one from data (empirical) or from theory (equally likely outcomes), and how the law of large numbers ties the two together.
title: Lesson 1 - Estimating Probabilities

content:
Welcome to Joins Up to now, every query you have written has pulled from a single table. Real databases do not work that way. They spread information across many tables on purpose, and the most useful questions almost always need data from more than one of them. The tool that brings those tables back together is the join.
Imagine you need a list of sales by customer that includes each customer&rsquo;s email address. The invoice table records sales, but it only stores a customer_id — not the email. The email lives in the customer table. A join lets you connect the two so you can see them side by side in a single result.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Combine data from two tables using an inner join Explain, step by step, how SQL processes a join Select specific columns from different tables and resolve ambiguous column names Alias tables (and columns) to keep your queries short and readable You will work with the Chinook database, a realistic model of a digital music …
summary: Combine data from multiple tables with inner joins, select columns across tables, and alias tables for clarity.
title: Lesson 1 - Introduction to Joins

content:
Welcome to Status Codes and Response Types Every HTTP response carries a three-digit status code — a number that tells the client what happened before it reads a single byte of the body. You&rsquo;ve already seen a few: 200 when things work, 422 when validation fails, 404 when something&rsquo;s missing. So far FastAPI has chosen these for you. In this lesson you take control: you&rsquo;ll learn what the codes mean and how to return the right one for each outcome, plus how to send responses that aren&rsquo;t JSON. Getting status codes right is one of the simplest things that separates a sloppy API from a professional one.
This lesson sets the foundation for the rest of the module — clean errors, forms, and files all build on speaking HTTP clearly.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Explain the HTTP status-code families (2xx, 4xx, 5xx) Set a custom status_code on a path operation (e.g. 201 Created) Use the status module instead of memorizing numbers Choose a response type …
summary: Make your API communicate clearly: return the right HTTP status code for each outcome and choose the right response type beyond plain JSON.
title: Lesson 1 - Status Codes and Response Types

content:
Welcome to Why LLMs Need Tools A language model is a brilliant text predictor, but it is sealed inside its own training data. It cannot see today&rsquo;s weather, read your database, call an API, or take any action in the world. It also can&rsquo;t reliably do exact arithmetic on big numbers — it predicts plausible digits, not computed ones. Tool use (also called function calling) is how you break that seal: you hand the model a set of functions it may call, and it decides when to use them.
In this lesson you&rsquo;ll see the limitation first-hand, then watch the model ask to use a tool you provide — your first complete round-trip.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Explain the three things a text-only model cannot do Describe what &ldquo;tool use&rdquo; actually is (the model asks; your code runs) Read a tool_use response and the tool_use stop reason Complete a full request → execute → respond loop You&rsquo;ll reuse the SDK setup from earlier modules. Let&rsquo;s begin. …
summary: See why a text-only model is limited — no live data, no reliable computation, no actions — and watch it reach for a tool you provide.
title: Lesson 1 - Why LLMs Need Tools

content:
This lesson map connects Introduction, What Are Classes and Objects?, and Adding Attributes. Introduction So far, we&rsquo;ve been working with Python&rsquo;s built-in data types like strings, lists, and dictionaries. While these are powerful, real-world applications often need custom data structures that better represent the things we&rsquo;re modeling. This is where Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) comes in.
Object-oriented programming is a programming paradigm that organizes code around objects rather than just functions and logic. An object bundles together data (called attributes) and the functions that work with that data (called methods).
Think of it this way: when you&rsquo;re building a bookstore application, you don&rsquo;t just want a bunch of disconnected lists of book titles, prices, and authors. You want a Book object that keeps all that information together and knows how to do things like calculate discounts or display itself nicely.
In this lesson, we&rsquo;ll learn: …
summary: Introduction to Object-Oriented Programming
title: Lesson 1 - Introduction to Object-Oriented Programming

Welcome to Source Freshness A source declaration is a promise: this data exists, and a model can trust it. dbt source freshness is how that promise gets checked on a schedule, not assumed forever. This lesson runs it against raw.trips twice — first with a choice that looks reasonable and is quietly wrong, then with the fix, tested through all three states a freshness check can report.

Configure loaded_at_field and warn_after/error_after thresholds on a source Explain why a business timestamp is usually the wrong choice for loaded_at_field Run dbt source freshness and read a PASS, a WARN, and an ERROR STALE result correctly A Plausible Mistake raw.trips already has a timestamp column: pickup_time, the moment each trip started. Welcome to Real Key Routing Module 2 Lesson 4 proved deterministic key routing with small, synthetic test keys — &quot;taxi-042&quot;, &quot;taxi-001&quot;, values invented for the demo. This lesson proves the same guarantee holds on cityflow-trip-events itself, with trip data, at a scale where the &ldquo;small sample, uneven spread&rdquo; caveat from that lesson stops applying — and then finds an easy-to-miss way that same-key-same-partition can silently break even when Kafka&rsquo;s own partitioner is working exactly as designed.

Welcome to Parquet Every file this course has read so far has been a CSV. Parquet is a different format entirely — columnar and compressed on disk, the same shape DuckDB already keeps data in once it&rsquo;s loaded, rather than a text file DuckDB has to parse line by line. This lesson writes a real Thistlewood Goods file to Parquet, reads it back, and verifies the round trip against the CSV original before looking at exactly what changed.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Write a query&rsquo;s result to a Parquet file with COPY ... TO ... (FORMAT PARQUET) Read a Parquet file directly, the same way you&rsquo;d read a CSV Verify a CSV-to-Parquet round trip two ways: row count and schema, then an independently computed aggregate State, with real numbers, why Parquet files are smaller than the CSVs they&rsquo;re built from This lesson&rsquo;s code was run against DuckDB 1.5.5, verified on 2026-08-12 — the version and date this whole course is pinned to. Welcome to Selecting Columns with pl.col Lesson 1 used pl.col(&quot;unit_price&quot;) without stopping to cover the full vocabulary. pl.col is the single most common piece of every expression you&rsquo;ll write for the rest of this course, and it has several forms beyond &ldquo;one column by name.&rdquo; This lesson runs every one of them against the 7-column Thistlewood product catalog and confirms exactly which columns come back.

Welcome to Operators Every task Module 2 wrote used PythonOperator (directly, or wrapped by @task) because every task was, underneath, &ldquo;run this Python function.&rdquo; That&rsquo;s not the only real choice. An operator is Airflow&rsquo;s word for what kind of work a task does — PythonOperator runs a Python callable, BashOperator runs a shell command, and dozens of others (covered later in this course) talk to specific systems. This lesson puts a real BashOperator next to a real PythonOperator in the same DAG and shows when each is the right tool.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Write a BashOperator task that runs a genuine shell command against a real file Explain why BashOperator&rsquo;s stdout becomes an XCom value the same way a PythonOperator&rsquo;s return value does Choose between PythonOperator and BashOperator based on what a task&rsquo;s job actually is, not habit One DAG, Two Kinds of Task cityflow_operators_demo_dag.py checks that CityFlow&rsquo;s real …

title: Lesson 2 - Operators

content:
Welcome to Multi-Stage Builds Lesson 1 ended on a warning: python:3.13-slim works for free only when every dependency ships a prebuilt wheel. This lesson hits the case where one doesn&rsquo;t. CityFlow&rsquo;s team needs a job that talks to Postgres directly with psycopg2 — not psycopg2-binary, the version that ships a wheel — and psycopg2 genuinely needs a C compiler and Postgres&rsquo;s own header files to install. You&rsquo;ll watch it fail on the slim image, fix it by adding a compiler, and then learn the pattern that lets you keep that compiler for the build without shipping it: a multi-stage build.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Explain why some Python dependencies need to compile from source, and recognize the failure when they can&rsquo;t. Write a Dockerfile with more than one FROM, and use COPY --from=&lt;stage&gt; to move files between stages. Distinguish what a build stage needs from what a runtime stage needs, for a real compiled dependency. Measure the …
summary: Compile a real dependency in one build stage, then ship only the compiled result in a second, measuring the real size win.
title: Lesson 2 - Multi-Stage Builds

content:
Welcome to Kinds of Checks In Lesson 1 you learned that the check matters most. This lesson is about the kinds of check you can build, because they&rsquo;re not all equal. Some give you a clean, objective yes or no; others depend on judgment and need more care to stay honest. Knowing the menu — and knowing which item fits the task in front of you — is the difference between a check that reliably catches problems and one that just feels like checking.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Name the main kinds of checks and what each is good for Pick the strongest check a given task allows Prefer objective checks where they exist, and use judgment-based ones only for the rest Recognize when a real-world signal is the check that actually counts Let&rsquo;s walk the menu from the most objective to the most judgment-based.
A Spectrum from Rules to Judgment Checks live on a spectrum. On one end are objective checks — a rule either passes or it doesn&rsquo;t, and any two people (or …
summary: Meet the main kinds of checks — hard rules, checklists, reference examples, rubrics, and real-world signals — and learn which one fits which job.
title: Lesson 2 - Kinds of Checks

content:
Welcome to Filtering &amp; Cleaning Lesson 1 gave you the Column object: select, withColumn, expressions, casts. You can now shape a DataFrame. This lesson is about shrinking one — deciding which rows deserve to survive — and it is the most dangerous thing CityFlow&rsquo;s engineers do all quarter. Filtering feels innocent. You write filter(total_amount &gt;= 0) because negative money &ldquo;looks wrong,&rdquo; the count drops a little, the code turns green, and you have just fabricated three million dollars of revenue that never existed. The taxi data is genuinely dirty — a pickup stamped in 2002, a single trip logged at 312,722 miles, three quarters of a million rows with missing passenger counts — and the engineer&rsquo;s whole job is telling dirt apart from data that merely offends a tidy instinct. Get that judgment wrong and every downstream number inherits the mistake.
So this lesson is not a syntax tour, though you will meet every filtering tool Spark has. It is a lesson in …
summary: Clean the real taxi dirt in Spark without corrupting it: the quarter window drops 21 stray rows, but dropping the 115,894 negative-total reversals invents $2,986,808.76 of revenue CityFlow never earned.
title: Lesson 2 - Filtering & Cleaning

content:
Welcome to Categoricals In Lesson 1 you downcast CityFlow&rsquo;s numeric columns, trading int64 for int16 and float64 for float32 wherever the values fit. That worked because a narrower number really is fewer bytes. But some of the heaviest columns in the taxi data are not numbers at all — they are labels that repeat endlessly. payment_type is one of five codes, printed 200,000 times. Once you join the zone lookup to get a readable pickup_borough name, that column is the word &quot;Manhattan&quot; (or one of six others) written out on nearly every row.
Storing the full label on every row is pure waste when there are only a handful of distinct labels. Pandas has a dtype built for exactly this situation: category. It stores each distinct value once, in a small shared table, and gives every row a tiny integer code that points into that table. For a column with few distinct values over many rows, the saving is large — and in this lesson you will measure it on the real taxi sample. You …
summary: Convert low-cardinality taxi columns like payment_type and pickup borough to the category dtype for large, measured memory savings — and see the case where a near-unique column makes category bigger, not smaller.
title: Lesson 2 - Categoricals

content:
Welcome to Splitting into Heads In the previous lesson you saw why a transformer wants several attention heads: each head can specialize, learning a different relationship between tokens. The obvious way to build that would be to keep h separate little projection matrices, run h separate attention calculations, and stack the results. It works, but it is clumsy, and it is not how real transformers (including the tiny char-level GPT you are building in this course) actually do it.
Instead they use one wide projection of shape (C, C) and then split the result into h heads with a reshape and a transpose. No extra matmuls, no Python loop over heads, just index arithmetic on a single tensor. This lesson is purely about that plumbing: how a (B, T, C) projection becomes a (B, h, T, hs) stack of independent per-head problems, and why the reshape and the transpose are each doing exactly what they need to.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Explain why real transformers use one (C, …
summary: Learn the reshape and transpose mechanics that turn one wide (C, C) projection into h parallel attention heads of size hs = C // h.
title: Lesson 2 - Splitting into Heads

content:
Welcome to Token-Level F1 &amp; Overlap Metrics In Lesson 1 you scored Docent &ndash; our assistant for the Meridian serverless database docs &ndash; with exact match: normalize both strings, then check whether they&rsquo;re identical. That gave you a fast, reproducible number, but it also gave you a harsh one. Exact match is a switch, not a dial. Docent can answer &quot;The rate limit returns HTTP status code 429&quot; when the reference is &quot;429&quot;, get the fact exactly right, and still score a flat 0, because the strings aren&rsquo;t identical. A completely wrong answer scores 0 too. Exact match cannot tell those two apart, and for question answering that&rsquo;s a real problem: most answers are neither perfect strings nor total nonsense &ndash; they&rsquo;re mostly right, and you want a metric that says so.
This lesson introduces the metric that gives partial credit: token-level F1, the same F1 the SQuAD reading-comprehension benchmark uses. Instead of comparing two strings …
summary: Learn token-level F1, the SQuAD partial-credit metric, and score real Docent answers where exact match gives a flat zero to a mostly-correct reply.
title: Lesson 2 - Token-Level F1 & Overlap Metrics

content:
Welcome to Cross-Validation with xgb.cv In Lesson 1 you learned to hand XGBoost a validation set and let early stopping halt training the moment that set stopped improving. That solved one problem: you no longer have to guess how many trees to grow. But it quietly introduced another. Your entire verdict about the model, both the tree count and the RMSE you reported, now rests on a single split of the data. Change which rows happen to fall into that validation set and the numbers move. Sometimes by more than the improvement you were trying to measure.
Northwind Analytics ran into exactly this. Two analysts each held out 20 percent of the California Housing districts to check the same XGBoost settings, got test RMSEs a couple hundredths apart, and spent an afternoon arguing about which configuration was &ldquo;better&rdquo; when the difference was pure luck of the draw. The fix is cross-validation: instead of trusting one split, you rotate through several, train on each, and average the …
summary: Use XGBoost's native xgb.cv to run 5-fold cross-validation on real California Housing data, let early stopping pick the tree count for you, and report an honest RMSE with its fold-to-fold standard deviation.
title: Lesson 2 - Cross-Validation with xgb.cv

content:
Welcome to Software Testing Fundamentals In the last lesson, Ledgerly&rsquo;s team rewrote a tangled pricing function into five small, well-named functions: calculate_subtotal, apply_tier_discount, apply_loyalty_discount, add_tax, and add_late_fee. Clean code answers one question: can a person read this and understand it? Testing answers a different question: does this code keep doing the right thing, today and after every future change?
Without automated tests, the only way to check calculate_invoice_total still works is to run Ledgerly by hand, create a fake customer, add line items, and read the number off the screen. That takes minutes, and a developer has to remember to do it every time they touch pricing code. This lesson replaces that manual check with automated tests that run in a fraction of a second, so Ledgerly&rsquo;s three-person team can change pricing logic without fear of quietly breaking a customer&rsquo;s bill.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Explain …
summary: Learn unit, integration, and end-to-end testing by writing real pytest tests for Ledgerly's invoice pricing functions and a fake payment gateway.
title: Lesson 2 - Software Testing Fundamentals

content:
Welcome to the Augmented Dickey-Fuller Test Lesson 1 compared Cyclepath&rsquo;s first-half and second-half statistics by hand and saw a clear mean shift. That was useful, but it is not a real answer to &ldquo;is this series stationary?&rdquo; It does not say how confident to be, and it would not work for a subtler case where the difference is small but still real. The Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test replaces that visual check with an actual statistical test: a single function call that returns a number and a p-value you can act on.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
State the ADF test&rsquo;s null and alternative hypotheses in terms of a &ldquo;unit root&rdquo; Run adfuller from statsmodels and read its output Interpret the p-value against the conventional 0.05 threshold Confirm formally that raw Cyclepath is non-stationary Let&rsquo;s run it.
What the Test Actually Asks The ADF test&rsquo;s hypotheses are usually stated in terms of a unit root. A unit root is a …
summary: The ADF test formalizes the stationarity question with a null hypothesis and a p-value. Run on raw Cyclepath, it returns p=0.7815 — nowhere near significant, confirming what Lesson 1 saw informally.
title: Lesson 2 - The Augmented Dickey-Fuller Test

content:
Welcome to Statistical Power Last lesson you met the two errors and learned that α, the false-positive rate, is a dial you set directly. Its counterpart, β — the chance you miss a real effect — is different: you don&rsquo;t set it, you buy it down. The quantity you actually design around isn&rsquo;t β itself but its complement, power = 1 − β: the probability that when there really is an effect, your test catches it. A test with low power is a test that will quietly kill real winners, and the frustrating part is you&rsquo;d never know — a non-significant result looks the same whether the effect was absent or just too small to see with the data you had. This lesson defines power precisely and walks through the four levers that move it, so that by the time you compute a sample size you understand exactly what you&rsquo;re purchasing.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Define power as 1 − β and explain the 80% convention Name the four levers that control power and which …
summary: Power is the probability your test detects a real effect — and four levers control it: effect size, sample size, significance level, and variance. Only two of those levers are truly free.
title: Lesson 2 - Statistical Power

Welcome to Validating Inputs with Pydantic In the last lesson you learned to write a tight, typed input_schema so Claude reaches for the right tool and provides the right arguments. But a schema is a guide, not a guarantee. Claude reads it and usually obeys it — yet the model can still send a value the schema didn&rsquo;t fully rule out, or that slips through because you forgot a constraint. When that bad value reaches your function, you get a crash, a wrong answer, or a silent corruption deep inside your code. This lesson adds a hard guarantee on top of the guide. You&rsquo;ll define a tool&rsquo;s inputs as a Pydantic model, generate the schema Claude sees from that same model, and validate every argument Claude sends — catching the bad ones before your function ever runs.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Define a tool&rsquo;s inputs as a Pydantic BaseModel with typed, constrained fields Generate the tool&rsquo;s input_schema directly from the model so the two never …
summary: Catch bad tool inputs before they reach your code — define inputs as a Pydantic model, generate the tool schema from it, and validate every argument Claude sends.
title: Lesson 2 - Validating Inputs with Pydantic

content:
Welcome to Defining Tools and Schemas In Lesson 1 you saw the whole tool-use loop in miniature: the model asked for a tool, you ran it, it answered. But that loop only works if the model can understand the tools you offer. A tool definition is the entire contract between you and the model — get it right and the model calls the correct function with valid arguments; get it vague and the model guesses, calls the wrong tool, or doesn&rsquo;t call anything at all.
In this lesson you&rsquo;ll write definitions the model can actually use, watch how a single word in a description changes its behavior, and learn to take direct control of when it reaches for a tool.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Write a clear name, a prescriptive description, and a precise input_schema Explain why the description is the part the model reads to decide when to call Build richer schemas with typed properties, enum, arrays, and required Offer multiple tools and steer selection with tool_choice …
summary: Write tool definitions the model can use reliably — a clear name, a prescriptive description, and a precise JSON schema — and watch it pick the right tool with valid arguments.
title: Lesson 2 - Defining Tools and Schemas

content:
Welcome to Handling Errors In the last lesson you learned to return the right status code when things go well. But real APIs spend a lot of their time on the unhappy paths: a client asks for a task that doesn&rsquo;t exist, tries to act on someone else&rsquo;s data, or sends a request that clashes with what&rsquo;s already there. When that happens, returning 200 OK with a confusing body is the worst thing you can do — the client thinks everything worked. A good API fails loudly and clearly, with a 4xx status code and a message that says exactly what went wrong.
FastAPI gives you two tools for this. The first, HTTPException, is a ready-made way to stop a request and return an error response with one line. The second, custom exception handlers, lets you catch your own error classes and turn them into clean HTTP responses in one central place — so your business logic stays readable and every error of a given kind looks the same. We&rsquo;ll build both on the Task Manager API from earlier …
summary: Return clean, correct errors: raise HTTPException with the right status code and a clear message, and write custom handlers that turn your own exceptions into tidy responses.
title: Lesson 2 - Handling Errors

Welcome to Joins with Other Clauses In the last lesson you combined two tables. But a join is rarely the whole query. You usually want to filter the combined rows, count them by group, or sort them — the same WHERE, GROUP BY, and ORDER BY clauses you already know. The good news is that they work on a joined result exactly as they do on a single table.
Say you have noticed monthly sales slipping and want to find out why. Answering that means combining several tables, filtering to a period, and aggregating the result. This lesson shows you how the pieces fit together.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Treat the result of a join as a temporary table you can query further Combine joins with LIMIT, WHERE, GROUP BY, and ORDER BY Join three or more tables in a single query State the order in which SQL executes its clauses You will keep working with the Chinook music-store database. Let&rsquo;s begin.
Data for this lesson
Database: chinook.db — a digital music store (SQLite). …
summary: Join more than two tables and see how joins work alongside WHERE, GROUP BY, and ORDER BY.
title: Lesson 2 - Joins with Filtering, Grouping, and Sorting

content:
Welcome to Merging In the last lesson you watched SkyLog&rsquo;s history fork: main and feature/colored-output each gained commits the other didn&rsquo;t have. Branching is only half the story, though — eventually you want that feature work back on main. That&rsquo;s what merging does. git merge takes the commits from one branch and brings them into the branch you&rsquo;re standing on. The part that trips people up is that Git has two ways of doing this depending on what the history looks like — a quiet fast-forward or a three-way merge that creates a brand-new merge commit. Once you can tell which one happened by reading the graph, merging stops feeling like magic.
We&rsquo;ll keep working in the SkyLog repository.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Merge one branch into another with git merge Tell a fast-forward merge from a three-way merge and explain why each happens Force a merge commit with --no-ff to keep feature history visible Read a merge in git log --oneline …
summary: Bring branches back together with git merge — understand fast-forward and three-way merges, force a merge commit with --no-ff, and clean up merged branches.
title: Lesson 2 - Merging

Welcome to Probability Rules In the last lesson you learned to put a number on chance — by counting how often something happens in data, and by counting equally likely outcomes in theory. That gives you the probability of a single event. But real questions rarely stop there. You want the chance of not something, or of one thing or another. To answer those, you need a small set of rules that combine probabilities reliably.
In this lesson you will give chance a precise vocabulary — sample spaces and events — see the handful of axioms every probability must obey, and then learn the two rules you will reach for constantly: the complement rule for &ldquo;not,&rdquo; and the addition rule for &ldquo;or.&rdquo; You will check every rule against real penguin data and against a fair die.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Describe a random experiment with a sample space and define events inside it State the probability axioms and use them to sanity-check any probability Apply the …
summary: Learn the language of sample spaces and events, the axioms every probability obeys, and the complement and addition rules for combining events.
title: Lesson 2 - Probability Rules

Welcome to Dependencies Every DAG so far has used &gt;&gt; to mean &ldquo;runs after&rdquo; — simple, but it&rsquo;s only one of four ways Airflow lets you say the same thing, and every DAG so far has also been a straight line: one task, then the next, then the next. This lesson does both things this course hasn&rsquo;t done yet: uses all four dependency mechanisms in one DAG, and wires a DAG whose dependency graph branches — two tasks with no edge between them, both feeding a third.

Welcome to Slimming Images Lessons 1 and 2 slimmed an image by choosing what goes into the FROM line and what a multi-stage build lets you leave behind. This lesson slims an image two more ways, both real and both easy to get wrong by accident: what a careless COPY . . drags in from your project folder, and how the number of layers an installation step uses can change the final size even when every layer installs exactly the same software.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Write a .dockerignore file and explain exactly what it prevents. Measure the real megabytes a bloated build context adds to an image. The setup: a real project folder, with real junk in it CityFlow&rsquo;s zone-revenue reporter is the same shape of job as Lesson 1&rsquo;s — but this time it lives in a real project folder, the way code …
