title: Lesson 1 - Feature Importance and Its Pitfalls

content:
Welcome to Version Control Essentials Ledgerly&rsquo;s three-person team edits the same files every week: Invoice, Customer, Subscription, and the rest of the codebase you met in earlier modules. Without a system for tracking who changed what, two developers editing invoice.py on the same afternoon would overwrite each other&rsquo;s work with no way to undo the damage. Version control is that system, and this lesson opens Module 4, &ldquo;Delivery &amp; Operations,&rdquo; with a short conceptual pass over it.
This lesson is deliberately brief. It gives you the mental model — commits, branches, remotes — and a handful of commands you will use every day, using real output from an actual git repository built for this lesson. It does not teach branching strategies, merge conflicts, rebasing, or pull request review in depth. Those topics belong to a full nine-module course, &ldquo;Version Control with Git and GitHub,&rdquo; linked later in this lesson, and this overview intentionally stays …
summary: A short conceptual overview of version control for the Ledgerly team: why it exists, what a commit represents, and how branches and a shared GitHub remote keep three developers from overwriting each other's work.
title: Lesson 1 - Version Control Essentials

content:
Welcome to What ACF and PACF Measure Module 3 (Stationarity and Differencing) left off with a stationary series and a preview. The ARIMA models in Module 5 (AR, MA, ARMA, ARIMA) need two numbers: how many autoregressive (AR) terms and how many moving-average (MA) terms. This module is where those numbers come from. The tool is a pair of functions with confusingly similar names: the autocorrelation function (ACF) and the partial autocorrelation function (PACF). They look at the same data and often produce similar-looking plots. But they answer genuinely different questions, and the difference between their answers is what makes order selection possible at all.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Define the ACF as the correlation between a series and its own lagged values Define the PACF as that same correlation with intermediate lags&rsquo; effects removed Explain, with a concrete example, why the two can disagree at the same lag Compute both on Cyclepath&rsquo;s stationary …
summary: The ACF measures raw correlation between a series and its own past; the PACF measures the same relationship with the effect of every intermediate lag stripped out. The difference between them is what tells an AR process from an MA process.
title: Lesson 1 - What ACF and PACF Measure

content:
Welcome to the Two-Proportion Z-Test Lumen ran the signup experiment you designed and sized. The results are in: out of 5,000 users each, the current page converted 503 and the new page converted 613 — 10.06% versus 12.26%. The new page looks better. But you already know the trap from Module 3: observed rates aren&rsquo;t true rates, and a gap this size could, in principle, be noise. So the question isn&rsquo;t &ldquo;which number is bigger&rdquo; — it&rsquo;s &ldquo;is this difference large enough that chance alone probably didn&rsquo;t produce it?&rdquo; The tool that answers it for proportions is the two-proportion z-test, and in this lesson you&rsquo;ll build it from its parts and run it on exactly this data.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Compute the difference in conversion rates and its pooled standard error Form the z statistic and explain what it measures Turn z into a two-sided p-value with scipy Run the full test on Lumen&rsquo;s experiment and read the …
summary: The data is in — now turn two conversion rates into a verdict. Build the two-proportion z-test from scratch: the difference, the pooled standard error, the z statistic, and the p-value — and run it on Lumen's signup experiment.
title: Lesson 1 - The Two-Proportion Z-Test

content:
Welcome to The Messages List Is Memory People often imagine &ldquo;agent memory&rdquo; as some special subsystem. It isn&rsquo;t — at least not the short-term kind. Look back at the agent loop you built: every turn, you append the model&rsquo;s response and the tool results to one list called messages, and you send that whole list on the next call. That list is the agent&rsquo;s memory. It&rsquo;s why the agent can refer to something from three steps ago: the entire history is right there in the prompt. Seeing this clearly is the key to the whole module, because it immediately reveals the two problems you&rsquo;ll spend the rest of it solving.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Explain why the messages list is the agent&rsquo;s short-term memory Identify the two problems with relying on it alone Distinguish short-term memory from long-term memory Describe what each kind of memory is good for This builds directly on the agent loop from Module 2. Let&rsquo;s begin.
Memory Is …

Welcome to Conditional Probability Most useful probabilities come with a condition attached. You rarely ask &ldquo;what is the chance of rain?&rdquo; in the abstract — you ask &ldquo;what is the chance of rain given that the sky is grey?&rdquo; The extra information changes the answer. Conditional probability is the tool for updating what you believe once you learn that something is true, and it is the single idea that everything in Bayesian reasoning is built on.
In this lesson you will make that idea concrete with a real dataset of penguins. You will condition on which island a penguin lives on, watch a probability move as you add that knowledge, and compute every number yourself in Python so the formula stops being abstract.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Explain what P(A∣B) P(A \mid B) means and read it as &ldquo;the probability of A given B&rdquo; Use the formula P(A∣B)=P(A∩B)/P(B) P(A \mid B) = P(A \cap B) / P(B) and compute it directly from data Show how …
summary: Learn what P(A given B) means, the formula behind it, and how to compute conditional probabilities from real data by restricting to a subgroup.
title: Lesson 1 - Conditional Probability Fundamentals

content:
Welcome to Dependency Injection As an API grows, the same little jobs show up in endpoint after endpoint: read the pagination parameters, check the caller is authenticated, open a database connection. Copy-pasting that logic into every function is how codebases rot — change one rule and you have to hunt down ten copies. FastAPI&rsquo;s answer is dependency injection: you write the shared logic once as a dependency, declare which endpoints need it with Depends, and FastAPI runs it for you and hands the result to your function. It&rsquo;s one of FastAPI&rsquo;s most loved features, and once it clicks you&rsquo;ll use it constantly.
This lesson introduces the core idea. The next lesson adds class dependencies, sub-dependencies, and setup/teardown with yield.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Explain what dependency injection is and the problem it solves Write a dependency function and inject it with Depends Reuse one dependency across multiple endpoints Describe why this …
summary: Share logic across endpoints without repeating yourself: write a dependency function once and inject it anywhere with Depends.
title: Lesson 1 - Dependency Injection

content:
Welcome to Scalar Subqueries Up to now, every query you have written has had a single job: pull rows from one place, maybe join, filter, and aggregate them, and return a result. But many real questions need the answer to one query in order to ask another. How does each country&rsquo;s sales compare to the total? Which invoices are above the company-wide average? These questions are awkward — or impossible — to answer in a single flat query.
The tool that solves this is the subquery: a query nested inside another query. In this lesson you will meet the simplest and most common kind, the scalar subquery, which returns exactly one value you can drop into a calculation or comparison.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Explain what a subquery is and why subqueries matter Write a scalar subquery that returns a single value Use a scalar subquery inside a SELECT calculation Filter rows with a scalar subquery in WHERE and HAVING Follow SQL style conventions for writing readable …
summary: Use a subquery that returns a single value to compare rows against a computed benchmark, and see why subqueries matter.
title: Lesson 1 - Scalar Subqueries

content:
Welcome to What GitHub Is and Creating a Repository So far, every repository you&rsquo;ve made lives only on your computer. That&rsquo;s fine for solo work — until your laptop dies, or you want to show someone your project, or work with a teammate. A remote solves this: it&rsquo;s a copy of your repository kept somewhere else that you sync with. GitHub is the most popular service for hosting remotes — a website that stores Git repositories, adds a friendly interface, and provides the collaboration features you&rsquo;ll use in the next module. This lesson explains how GitHub relates to the Git you already know, how to create a repository on it, and how your computer authenticates to it.
Remember from Module 1: Git is the tool on your machine; GitHub is an online host for Git repositories. They work together.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Explain what GitHub is and how local and remote repositories relate Create a new repository on GitHub Describe the difference between …

Welcome to What MCP Is and Why It Matters In Module 3 you gave a model tools by writing schemas and running the tool-use loop yourself. It worked — but think about what happens at scale. Every team writes its own integration to the same GitHub, the same database, the same file system. A tool you build for your chatbot can&rsquo;t be reused by your IDE or by Claude Desktop, because each app has its own private way of defining tools. That duplicated effort is exactly the problem the Model Context Protocol (MCP) was created to solve.
This lesson is about the idea and the architecture. The next lessons get hands-on.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Explain what MCP is and the problem it solves Describe the roles of hosts, clients, and servers List the three things an MCP server can expose Explain why &ldquo;build once, use anywhere&rdquo; matters There&rsquo;s no setup yet — just one quick look at a server&rsquo;s tools. Let&rsquo;s begin.

Welcome to Volumes Every Postgres container you&rsquo;ve run so far in this course has been short-lived — created, used, torn down within a single lesson. Lesson 1&rsquo;s db never outlived its own docker compose down. That&rsquo;s fine for a smoke test, but a real database has to survive far more ordinary events: a container restart, an image upgrade, a docker compose down you run on purpose to free up resources before running up again ten minutes later. This lesson answers a direct, concrete question: when a Postgres container is removed and a new one takes its place, what happens to the data — and what&rsquo;s the one line in a Compose file that changes the answer?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Explain where a container&rsquo;s writable filesystem lives, and why it disappears when the container is removed. Declare a named volume in a Compose file and mount it at a service&rsquo;s data directory. Predict, correctly, whether a given Compose file will lose or keep …

Welcome to Persistent Setup In Lesson 1 you kept a loop from drifting by re-anchoring the brief. This lesson removes the retyping entirely: instead of pasting your brief and check into every new chat, you store them once, so every conversation starts already anchored. Both ChatGPT and Claude offer a feature for this — a Project — plus custom instructions that apply everywhere. For a loop you run regularly, like Harborlight&rsquo;s weekly newsletter, this turns a cold start into a warm one, every time.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Explain what a Project stores and why it helps a recurring loop Put a brief, a check, and reference files into a persistent setup Use custom instructions for preferences that apply to everything Decide what belongs in persistent setup versus a single chat Let&rsquo;s start with the idea of persistent setup.
Setup That Sticks Around Everything you&rsquo;ve learned so far — the brief, the definition of done — has been something you write and …
summary: Stop retyping your brief and check. Save them into a Project or custom instructions so every new chat starts already anchored to your goal and criteria.
title: Lesson 2 - Persistent Setup: Projects & Instructions

content:
Welcome to Reading .explain() Lesson 1 proved something that should reframe how you read your own code: the zone-hour report you wrote in Module 3 as a chain of DataFrame calls, and the same report written as a SQL string against a temp view, compile to a byte-identical physical plan. Both are just two ways of describing work to Catalyst, Spark&rsquo;s optimizer, and Catalyst decides what actually runs. Which raises the obvious next question — the one this whole module turns on. If the engine, not your syntax, decides the work, then you need to be able to read what it decided. Otherwise you are flying an instrument you can&rsquo;t see.
That instrument is .explain(), and this lesson makes you fluent in it. By the end you should be able to look at any node in a real Spark plan and say, out loud, what it does — which columns it reads, whether a filter got handed to the file format, where rows have to move between partitions, and which stage each piece of work belongs to. We&rsquo;ll do it …
summary: Read a real Spark physical plan node by node — FileScan to Exchange to final HashAggregate — and learn the four plan trees that .explain(mode=extended) prints, on CityFlow's 240,917-bucket zone-hour report.
title: Lesson 2 - Reading .explain()

content:
Welcome to Streaming Aggregation In Lesson 1 you learned to stream a file too big for RAM: pd.read_csv(chunksize=...) and pyarrow&rsquo;s iter_batches hand you the data one small piece at a time, and you counted all 2,964,624 rows of the January parquet with a footprint that never grew with the file. But counting rows is the easy case. The moment CityFlow&rsquo;s dashboard asks a real question — what is the average fare? — you hit a wall that looks fatal: the obvious answer is taxi[&quot;fare_amount&quot;].mean(), and .mean() seems to need the whole column in memory at once. If you only ever hold one chunk, how can you average a column you never fully assemble?
The way through is a small but powerful shift in how you think about an aggregate. A mean is not atomic. It is a ratio: total sum divided by total count. And a sum, unlike a mean, does break apart cleanly — the sum of the whole column is just the sum of each chunk&rsquo;s sum. So you can walk the file chunk by chunk, add each …
summary: Compute means, sums, counts, and group-by aggregates over data too big for RAM by accumulating partial (sum, count) results chunk by chunk, proven equal to the whole-file answer on the real NYC taxi data.
title: Lesson 2 - Streaming Aggregation

content:
Welcome to Token Embeddings Your mini-GPT reads text as integers. The tokenizer already turned the Lantern Bay corpus into a stream of ids in the range 0 to 23, one per character. But a neural network cannot multiply an integer id by a weight matrix and expect anything meaningful, the id 19 for the letter t is not &ldquo;nineteen times bigger&rdquo; than the id 0 for a space. Ids are labels, not magnitudes. The first thing a transformer does with a token id is look up a vector for it, and that vector is learned. This lesson builds that lookup: the token embedding table, the very first parameter block of the model.
An embedding table is the simplest layer in the whole course to run forward, it is literally an array index, but its backward pass hides a small, important surprise. Because the same token appears many times in a sequence, and its row is reused every time, the gradient for that row is not one value but a sum over all its occurrences. That summation is called a scatter-add, …
summary: Build the embedding table that turns token ids into learned vectors: a row lookup forward, a scatter-add backward, verified with a numerical gradient check in NumPy.
title: Lesson 2 - Token Embeddings

content:
Welcome to Rubric &amp; Direct Scoring In Lesson 1 you handed a hard-to-grade answer to a model and got back a single verdict: correct or incorrect. That binary is the right tool when there genuinely is one right answer and you just need a yes/no. But most of what Docent &ndash; our assistant for the Meridian serverless database docs &ndash; produces isn&rsquo;t a coin flip. An answer can be factually right yet invent a detail the docs never mention. It can be perfectly grounded yet so vague it doesn&rsquo;t actually help. &ldquo;Correct or not&rdquo; flattens all of that into one bit and throws away the shape of the failure.
The instinct is to ask for a number instead: &ldquo;rate this answer from 1 to 5.&rdquo; Try it and you&rsquo;ll watch it drift. Ask twice and you get a 4 then a 3 for the same answer; ask about two different answers and the model&rsquo;s private, unstated idea of what &ldquo;4&rdquo; means has quietly moved between them. A bare numeric scale is noisy because …
summary: Turn a noisy 'rate this 1-5' into reliable, explainable scores: build a three-criterion rubric for Docent answers and a judge that returns structured per-criterion JSON with a rationale.
title: Lesson 2 - Rubric & Direct Scoring

content:
Welcome to CI/CD and DevOps Ledgerly&rsquo;s three-person team now has a clean, tested codebase. Module 3 gave them pricing.py and nine automated tests that catch pricing regressions in a fraction of a second. Lesson 1 of this module showed how the team uses Git to track every change and review it before merging. This lesson connects those two pieces: instead of a developer remembering to run the tests by hand, a pipeline runs them automatically on every commit, and only lets tested code move toward real customers.
This automatic pipeline, and the practices around it, go by two names you will hear constantly in a software job: CI/CD and DevOps. CI/CD is the technical machinery. DevOps is the way a team works so that machinery actually gets used well. You will build a real pipeline definition for Ledgerly, run a Python script that behaves like one pipeline stage, and watch it genuinely pass and genuinely fail, using the same pricing code from Module 3.
By the end of this lesson, you …
summary: Learn continuous integration and continuous delivery by building a GitHub Actions pipeline for Ledgerly and a Python script that fails the build the moment a real test breaks.
title: Lesson 2 - CI/CD and DevOps

content:
Welcome to Explaining Predictions with SHAP In Lesson 1 you learned to ask XGBoost which features matter, and you also learned to distrust the easy answer. The built-in gain, weight, and cover importances each tell a slightly different story, and none of them tells you why a single prediction came out the way it did. When Northwind Analytics hands a stakeholder a predicted median house value of 0.46 for one California district and the stakeholder asks &ldquo;why so low?&rdquo;, a global importance bar chart is no help at all. It describes the model in the aggregate; it cannot decompose one row.
This lesson gives you a tool that can. SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) attributes each individual prediction to its features, fairly and with a precise mathematical guarantee. It answers both questions at once: the global one (&ldquo;which features drive the model overall?&rdquo;) in a way that is more consistent than Lesson 1&rsquo;s importances, and the local one (&ldquo;why this exact …
summary: Use SHAP with TreeExplainer to explain XGBoost's California Housing predictions, verify the additivity property on real rows, and read both global and per-district feature contributions.
title: Lesson 2 - Explaining Predictions with SHAP

content:
Welcome to Reading the Signatures: AR vs MA Lesson 1 established that the ACF and PACF answer different questions, and that the gap between them is informative. This lesson puts that to use. There is a well-known pair of signatures, one for autoregressive (AR) processes and one for moving-average (MA) processes, where the ACF and PACF behave like mirror images of each other. Once you can recognize both shapes on data where you already know the right answer, reading them on a real, unknown series (Lesson 4) stops being guesswork.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
State the AR signature: ACF tails off, PACF cuts off sharply after lag p State the MA signature: ACF cuts off sharply after lag q, PACF tails off Recognize both signatures on synthetic data with known structure Explain the intuition for why each process produces its particular shape Let&rsquo;s build two processes where the answer is known in advance.
The AR Signature: ACF Tails Off, PACF Cuts Off An AR(1) process …
summary: An AR process's ACF tails off gradually while its PACF cuts off sharply; an MA process is the mirror image. Demonstrated on synthetic AR(1) and MA(1) series with known structure, the textbook signatures show up exactly as advertised.
title: Lesson 2 - Reading the Signatures: AR vs MA

content:
Welcome to Reading the P-Value Last lesson you built the two-proportion z-test and it handed Lumen a number: p = 0.00048. It&rsquo;s tempting to file that away as &ldquo;the probability the result was a fluke&rdquo; and move on — but that reading is wrong, and the wrong reading is exactly how teams talk themselves into believing weak results and dismissing real ones. A p-value is a precise thing that answers a narrow question, and almost every everyday phrasing of it says something the p-value doesn&rsquo;t. In this lesson you&rsquo;ll learn to read the number honestly: what it is, the four things it isn&rsquo;t, the threshold you compare it to, and how the one-sided-versus-two-sided choice changes it — worked on two Lumen experiments that give opposite verdicts.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
State precisely what a p-value is — and name the four misinterpretations to avoid Apply the p-versus-α decision rule and explain what &ldquo;not significant&rdquo; does and …
summary: You have a p-value — now read it honestly. What a p-value means, the four misinterpretations that fool teams, the significance threshold, and one-sided vs two-sided tests, worked on two contrasting Lumen experiments.
title: Lesson 2 - Reading the P-Value

content:
Welcome to Managing Context: Truncation and Budgets In the last lesson you saw the first problem with relying on the messages list as memory: it grows without bound. Every turn appends more, you resend the whole thing, and eventually the conversation no longer fits the context window — or the cost and latency climb past what you want to pay. This lesson tackles that head-on with the simplest tool available: truncation. You decide how much history to keep, drop the rest, and watch a token budget so you know when to trim. You&rsquo;ll also learn the one accurate way to measure how big your prompt really is.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Name the three strategies for keeping context inside the window, and when each fits Write a truncate_history function that keeps the first message and the most recent turns Reason about what truncation throws away — and when that&rsquo;s fine Measure prompt size accurately with Claude&rsquo;s count_tokens and manage a token budget Avoid …
summary: Keep the messages list inside the context window by truncating old turns and watching a token budget — and learn to measure prompt size accurately with count_tokens.
title: Lesson 2 - Managing Context: Truncation and Budgets

content:
Welcome to Conditional Probability, Intermediate In the last lesson you learned what conditional probability means: how knowing that one event happened reshapes the probability of another. This lesson turns that idea into machinery you can actually compute with. You will chain conditional probabilities through multi-stage problems, use them to decide whether two events are truly independent, and finish with the law of total probability — the rule that stitches a handful of conditional probabilities back into one unconditional answer.
That last rule is more than a curiosity. It is exactly the denominator that Bayes&rsquo; theorem needs in the next lesson, so the work you do here is the foundation for everything that follows. We will keep using the Palmer penguins, and add a deck of cards when we need a clean second example.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Apply the general multiplication rule P(A∩B)=P(B) P(A∣B) P(A \cap B) = P(B)\,P(A \mid B) and chain it through a …
summary: Chain conditional probabilities with the general multiplication rule, test independence, and recover an unconditional probability with the law of total probability.
title: Lesson 2 - Conditional Probability: Intermediate

Welcome to Connecting Local to Remote In Lesson 1 you created an empty repository on GitHub and learned how local and remote copies relate. Right now those two halves don&rsquo;t know about each other: your SkyLog project sits on your laptop with all its commits, and the GitHub repo sits online, empty and waiting. This lesson joins them. You&rsquo;ll register the remote with your local repo, publish your commits with your first git push, and set up a tracking link so every push after that is a single short command.
We&rsquo;ll keep using the SkyLog project and its GitHub repo. The remote&rsquo;s URL is git@github.com:datatweets/skylog.git (the SSH form; the HTTPS form would be https://github.com/datatweets/skylog.git).
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Register a remote with git remote add origin &lt;url&gt; and inspect it with git remote -v Explain why origin is the conventional name for your main remote Publish your work with git push -u origin main and explain what -u …
summary: Wire your local repository to a remote with git remote, then publish it with your first git push and an upstream-tracking branch.
title: Lesson 2 - Connecting Local to Remote

Welcome to Connecting to MCP Servers In Lesson 1 you saw a list of tools appear from a server and learned the host/client/server model behind it. Now you&rsquo;ll write the code that produces that list. By the end you&rsquo;ll have a working MCP client in Python that launches a server, shakes hands with it, asks what tools it offers, and calls one — the exact sequence a host runs under the hood.
We&rsquo;ll use the official MCP Python SDK for the client and a tiny FastMCP server so this lesson runs on its own. The next lesson goes deeper on building servers; here the server is just something for the client to talk to.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Explain MCP transports and why stdio is the default for local servers Launch a server and open a session with the Python MCP client Discover a server&rsquo;s tools with list_tools and call one with call_tool Describe the Anthropic MCP connector as the production path for remote servers You&rsquo;ll need the mcp and anthropic …

title: Lesson 2 - Connecting to MCP Servers

content:
Welcome to Multi-Row and Multi-Column Subqueries A scalar subquery hands you one value. But many questions need a set of values — &ldquo;which tracks belong to any of these genres?&rdquo; — or even a whole table — &ldquo;what is the average of each genre&rsquo;s longest track?&rdquo; For those, you need subqueries that return multiple rows or multiple columns.
In this lesson you will write multi-row subqueries that feed list operators like IN and NOT IN, and multi-column subqueries that stand in for tables in the FROM clause and in joins.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Write a multi-row subquery that returns several values in one column Filter rows with IN and NOT IN against a subquery Write a multi-column subquery that returns a table Use a subquery as a table in the FROM clause Join a subquery to a table or to another subquery You should already understand scalar subqueries from Lesson 1. Let&rsquo;s begin.

content:
Welcome to Reusable and Sub-Dependencies In the last lesson, a dependency was a single function that returned a value. That&rsquo;s the foundation, but real applications need more. Sometimes you want a dependency to hand back a typed object instead of a loose dictionary. Sometimes one piece of shared logic needs another piece of shared logic underneath it — checking the current user requires first checking the API key. And sometimes a dependency manages a resource that must be opened before the request and closed after it, like a database session.
FastAPI handles all three with the same Depends you already know. This lesson covers the patterns that take you from &ldquo;I can share a function&rdquo; to &ldquo;I can structure the shared layer of a real Task Manager API.&rdquo; We&rsquo;ll go one pattern at a time, show the code, run it, and read the actual output.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Use a class as a dependency to get a typed object back from Depends() Build a …
summary: Level up dependencies: use classes for typed dependencies, build dependencies on top of other dependencies, and manage setup and teardown with yield.
title: Lesson 2 - Reusable and Sub-Dependencies

Welcome to Singular Tests Lesson 2&rsquo;s four generic tests all take the same shape: a column, and a reusable rule. Some business rules don&rsquo;t fit that shape — they need a query written for that one specific claim. dbt calls that a singular test: a .sql file in tests/, nothing more.

Welcome to Offsets and Commits A committed offset is the only thing separating &ldquo;this consumer group has read message 47&rdquo; from &ldquo;this consumer group will read message 47 again the next time it starts.&rdquo; Every consumer this course has built so far let enable_auto_commit&rsquo;s default handle this quietly. This lesson turns it off, on purpose, and reproduces a real duplicate delivery to show exactly what that default was protecting against.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Explain what a committed offset actually represents Reproduce a real duplicate delivery caused by auto-commit&rsquo;s timing Fix it with manual, per-message commits State precisely what &ldquo;at-least-once&rdquo; delivery promises, and doesn&rsquo;t Auto-Commit, With a Long Interval On Purpose Produce 20 messages, then consume all of them with enable_auto_commit=True but auto_commit_interval_ms=60000 — a full minute, deliberately longer than this demo takes:
# gate: setup: docker …

DuckDB has a second kind of named, queryable object: a view — something that looks like a table when you query it, but stores no data of its own. This lesson builds a view and a table from the identical query, then proves the difference the only way that actually settles it: change the underlying data and watch which one updates.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Create a view with CREATE VIEW ... Welcome to Handling Missing Data Safely Lesson 1 found 9 null city values and 6 null email values in thistlewood_orders_raw.csv. is_null(), fill_null(), and drop_nulls() are the three obvious tools — but which one is right depends entirely on the column and what the missing value means. This lesson works through that decision carefully, and lands on a fix better than either a placeholder or a drop: recovering the true value from data this file already has access to.

Welcome to Loops Over Documents So far your loops have produced short things — a newsletter, an email. This lesson scales up to loops that work over documents: a long report to summarize, a stack of customer feedback to theme, a policy to rewrite. Two challenges appear at this size. First, the input can be too big to handle well in one pass. Second — and more usefully — the document gives you a powerful new kind of check: you can verify that the output actually traces back to the source, catching the invented details that plague AI summaries.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Break a document too big for one pass into checkable passes Use summarize-then-refine loops over long inputs Turn the source document into a ground-truth check against invented claims Recognize when to upload and reference rather than paste Let&rsquo;s start with the size problem.

content:
Welcome to Catalyst&rsquo;s Optimizations Lesson 2 taught you to read a physical plan node by node: you can now point at a FileScan, a Filter, a HashAggregate, an Exchange and say what each one does. But every plan you read there arrived pre-optimized. Between the query you typed and the plan Spark ran sits Catalyst, and Catalyst had already rewritten your code before .explain() ever printed it — pruned columns you didn&rsquo;t prune, pushed filters you wrote at the top down into the scan, folded arithmetic you left for later. This lesson makes that invisible rewriting visible by putting two plans side by side: the plan as you wrote it, and the plan Spark actually runs. The difference between them is Catalyst&rsquo;s whole job.
CityFlow&rsquo;s team is about to lean on that job. In Course 1 they hand-tuned everything: pruned columns by passing a columns= list to pyarrow, pushed filters by hand, built indexes to skip rows. Spark promises to do that automatically — and mostly it …
summary: Diff Catalyst's plans on the real taxi month: column pruning shrinks ReadSchema from 19 columns to 3 and cuts scanned bytes 2.52x, a pushed PULocationID filter skips zero row groups on a stats-less file so all 2,964,624 rows are still read, and a partitioned parquet you write …
title: Lesson 3 - Catalyst's Optimizations

content:
Welcome to SQLite as a Local Warehouse In Lesson 2 you learned to stream the full month of trips through pandas in chunks, computing a result without ever holding all 2.96 million rows in memory at once. That technique is exactly right for a one-pass job. But look at what it costs when CityFlow&rsquo;s dashboard needs five different numbers from the same month: each one re-opens the 50 MB parquet file, re-decodes every batch, and re-streams all 2,964,624 rows from scratch. You pay the full read five times to answer five questions. Streaming has no memory between runs.
This lesson fixes that with a better pattern for repeated queries: stream the data in once, into a real database on disk, then query it as many times as you like. The database is SQLite — a genuine, serverless, file-based SQL engine that ships inside Python&rsquo;s standard library as the sqlite3 module. There is nothing to install and no server to start; a database is just a file. You will stream the month into a trips …
summary: Stream a full month of NYC taxi trips into a local SQLite database with stdlib sqlite3, then run fast SQL GROUP BY and indexed WHERE queries over 2.96M on-disk rows without ever loading them all into pandas.
title: Lesson 3 - SQLite as a Local Warehouse

content:
Welcome to Sinusoidal Positional Encoding In the last lesson you saw the problem: self-attention is permutation-equivariant. Shuffle the tokens in a sequence and the attention output shuffles the same way, because attention treats its input as a set, not an ordered list. But &ldquo;the lamp keeper lights the lantern&rdquo; and &ldquo;the lantern lights the lamp keeper&rdquo; are made of the same characters and mean very different things. Our mini-GPT has to know where each token sits.
This lesson builds the answer the original Transformer used: sinusoidal positional encoding. It is a fixed, parameter-free formula that turns a position index like 0, 1, 2, ... into a vector the same width as a token embedding, (T, C). You add that vector onto the token embeddings, and suddenly every token carries a fingerprint of its position. No weights to learn, no lookup table to store, and it keeps working at sequence lengths you never trained on.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Write …
summary: Build the original Transformer's fixed sinusoidal positional encoding from scratch in NumPy and see why it gives every token a unique, bounded, extrapolatable sense of position.
title: Lesson 3 - Sinusoidal Positional Encoding

Welcome to Pairwise Comparison &amp; Preference In Lesson 2 you handed the judge one Docent answer and a rubric and asked for a score &ndash; an absolute number like 4 out of 5. That works, but it leans on the model having a stable, well-calibrated internal scale, and models don&rsquo;t really have one: ask the same judge to score the same answer on Monday and Friday and the number drifts. There is a more reliable question you can ask a judge, and it&rsquo;s the one this lesson is about: given these two answers to the same question, which one is better?
That shift &ndash; from absolute scoring to relative comparison &ndash; matters because both humans and models are markedly more consistent at relative judgements than absolute ones. You may not be able to say whether a wine is &ldquo;an 8&rdquo; but you can reliably say you prefer this glass to that one. Pairwise comparison is the backbone of preference evaluation: it powers the human-preference datasets used to align models, and …
summary: Judge Docent by asking a model which of two answers is better, aggregate into a win-rate, and defeat position bias by running both orders on real claude-haiku-4-5 calls.

Welcome to Hyperparameter Tuning with Optuna In Module 2&rsquo;s guided project, Northwind Analytics tuned XGBoost the way most people first learn to: with grid search and random search. Those got the job done, but they left a bad taste. Grid search made the team enumerate every combination by hand and watched the number of fits explode the moment they added a fourth or fifth hyperparameter. Random search was faster but felt like throwing darts in the dark, since each new setting was drawn without any memory of how the earlier ones scored.
In this lesson you will replace that guesswork with a smarter approach: Optuna, a modern hyperparameter-optimization library whose default sampler uses Bayesian optimization (specifically a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator, or TPE) to learn from every trial it has already run and steer the next one toward promising settings. You will tune XGBoost on the real California Housing data using a proper three-way split, tune only on the validation set, and …
summary: Tune XGBoost on the real California Housing data with Optuna's Bayesian TPE search, then confirm the winner on a held-out test set and compare it honestly against a default-XGBoost baseline.
title: Lesson 3 - Hyperparameter Tuning with Optuna

Welcome to Security Best Practices Ledgerly stores customer emails, invoice amounts, and a payment gateway API key. Every one of those is worth stealing. An attacker does not need to break into a server to get them. Often, a single unguarded input field is enough. This lesson shows the three-person Ledgerly team how to close the gaps that matter most: unsafe database queries, secrets sitting in source code, database accounts with more power than they need, and dependencies with known flaws.
This lesson closes out the technical content of the Delivery and Operations module. Earlier lessons in this module covered deploying Ledgerly and keeping it running. This lesson adds the last piece: keeping it safe while it runs. The guided project that follows brings deployment, monitoring, and security together into one end-to-end exercise.

Welcome to Confidence Bands and Multiple Testing Every ACF and PACF plot you will see, including every one in this module, comes with a shaded band. It is tempting to read it as a simple rule: bars inside the band do not matter, bars outside do. That is mostly right, but there is a real trap hiding in &ldquo;mostly&rdquo;. Test enough lags, and pure chance alone will occasionally push a bar outside the band even when there is genuinely nothing there. This lesson gives you the actual formula behind the band, and then proves the trap is real with a simulation.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
State the formula for the standard ACF/PACF significance band and what it assumes Explain what &ldquo;significant at this lag&rdquo; actually means statistically Recognize the multiple-testing problem and quantify how often it produces false alarms Apply healthy skepticism to an isolated significant spike with no independent explanation Let&rsquo;s start with where the band comes …
summary: The 1.96 over root-n band marks which ACF/PACF bars are statistically significant against pure white noise, but testing many lags at once means some bars cross that line by chance alone. A simulation shows 42% of pure noise series trip at least one 'significant' spike out of 15 …
title: Lesson 3 - Confidence Bands and Multiple Testing

Welcome to Confidence Intervals for the Difference The z-test told Lumen the new signup page beats the old one — p = 0.00048, not noise. But &ldquo;not noise&rdquo; isn&rsquo;t a plan. Before anyone ships, product wants to know how much better: is this a rounding-error win worth skipping, or a real lift worth the migration cost? A p-value can&rsquo;t answer that. It&rsquo;s a yes/no verdict that throws away the one number the decision actually hinges on — the size of the effect. The confidence interval puts that number back. Instead of &ldquo;the effect is real,&rdquo; it says &ldquo;the true lift is plausibly somewhere between here and here.&rdquo; In this lesson you&rsquo;ll build the 95% CI for the difference in two proportions, run it on Lumen&rsquo;s data, and see how it lines up exactly with the p-value from Lesson 1.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Build a 95% confidence interval for the difference in two proportions Explain why the CI uses the unpooled standard …
summary: A p-value says an effect is real; a confidence interval says how big it plausibly is. Build the 95% CI for the difference in two proportions with the unpooled standard error, and see how it agrees with the p-value.
title: Lesson 3 - Confidence Intervals for the Difference

Welcome to Summarization Memory Truncation keeps the list small by throwing the oldest turns away. That works when only the recent turns matter — but it&rsquo;s lossy. The moment a detail from early in the conversation becomes relevant again (&ldquo;what was that budget you mentioned at the start?&rdquo;), it&rsquo;s simply gone. Summarization takes a different bargain: instead of discarding the old turns, it compresses them. When the history gets long, you replace the old turns with one short summary of them and keep the recent turns in full. The list stays small, but the gist of the whole conversation survives.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Explain how summarization compresses old turns into a single summary message Write a compact_history function that folds everything except the last few turns into one summary Describe where the summary text comes from — a cheap model call Choose between truncation and summarization for a given situation This builds on the …
summary: Compress a long conversation instead of discarding it — fold old turns into a short summary while keeping recent turns in full, so the agent keeps the gist affordably.
title: Lesson 3 - Summarization Memory

Welcome to Bayes&rsquo; Theorem In the last lesson you saw that P(A∣B) P(A \mid B) and P(B∣A) P(B \mid A) are not the same number. That raises an obvious question: if you happen to know one of them, can you recover the other? Often you can — and Bayes&rsquo; theorem is the formula that does it. It is one of the most useful results in all of statistics, the engine behind spam filters, medical diagnosis, and the machine-learning classifier you will build in the next lesson.
In this lesson you will derive Bayes&rsquo; theorem from the conditional-probability formula you already know, learn the four names every Bayesian calculation uses, and work the famous medical-test problem in Python. The answer will surprise you.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Derive Bayes&rsquo; theorem from the definition of conditional probability Name the prior, likelihood, evidence, and posterior in any problem Compute a posterior probability in Python, including the full medical-test example …
summary: Derive Bayes' theorem from conditional probability, learn the prior-likelihood-posterior-evidence vocabulary, and work the famous medical-test problem in Python.
title: Lesson 3 - Bayes' Theorem

Welcome to Bigger Applications with Routers Every FastAPI project starts the same way: a single main.py with a handful of endpoints. That&rsquo;s perfect for learning and for tiny services. But the Task Manager you&rsquo;ve been building keeps growing — tasks, then users, then projects, then comments — and that one file balloons to hundreds of lines. Scrolling to find an endpoint becomes a chore, merge conflicts pile up when two people edit the same file, and the structure no longer tells you anything about how the app is organized. FastAPI&rsquo;s answer is the APIRouter: a way to group related routes into their own module, then plug that module into your app. Think of a router as a mini FastAPI app that holds a slice of your endpoints.
In this lesson you&rsquo;ll take routes out of main.py, give them a shared URL prefix and a docs tag, and reassemble everything with one line. The result behaves identically to the single-file version — the split is purely about organization.

Welcome to Nested and Correlated Subqueries So far your subqueries have run on their own — you could copy the inner query out, run it, and get a result independent of the outer query. In this lesson you will meet two more powerful patterns. A correlated subquery depends on the outer query and runs once per outer row. A nested subquery lives inside another subquery, letting you reach across three or more tables.
These are not new types of subquery — a correlated or nested subquery can still be scalar, multi-row, or multi-column. They are new ways of connecting subqueries to the queries around them.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Recognize and write a correlated subquery that references the outer query Use the EXISTS and NOT EXISTS operators Nest a subquery inside another subquery, several levels deep Apply a systematic approach to building complex subquery solutions You should be comfortable with scalar, multi-row, and multi-column subqueries from Lessons 1 and 2. …

Welcome to Syncing with Fetch, Pull, and Push In the last lesson you connected your local SkyLog repository to a remote and pushed it for the first time. But a remote is only useful if both sides stay current: you send your new commits up, and you bring teammates&rsquo; commits down. That two-way flow is what &ldquo;syncing&rdquo; means, and Git gives you a small set of commands to control it precisely — including one that lets you look before you leap.
The key insight of this lesson is that downloading changes and merging them are two separate steps. git fetch quietly downloads what&rsquo;s new without touching a single file you&rsquo;re working on. git pull downloads and merges in one move. Knowing the difference lets you decide when to peek first and when to just integrate.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

Introduction As your Python programs grow larger, keeping all your code in a single file becomes unwieldy and difficult to maintain. Welcome to UDFs &amp; Their Cost The last three lessons all rested on a single fact: Catalyst can optimize your query because it understands it. It knows filter(col(&quot;trip_distance&quot;) &gt;= 10) is a comparison, so it can push that comparison into the file scan; it knows select drops columns, so it can prune them; it knows groupBy(...).sum(...) is an aggregation, so it can pre-aggregate on each partition before the shuffle. Every optimization you have watched depends on the engine being able to see inside the operation. This lesson is about the operation Catalyst cannot see inside: a user-defined function, a chunk of your own Python that the optimizer must treat as a black box — feed it rows, take back results, and understand nothing about what happened in between.
That opacity has a price, and the price is measurable. You&rsquo;ll take one honest task — sorting January&rsquo;s 2,964,624 trips into distance tiers — and express it three ways: a built-in F.when expression, the …

Welcome to Incremental &amp; Resumable Pipelines In Lesson 3 you streamed a month of NYC taxi trips into a local SQLite warehouse a chunk at a time, never holding the whole file in memory. That works beautifully the first time. But a real pipeline does not run once — it runs again and again. January&rsquo;s data lands, you load it. A month later February&rsquo;s file appears, and you run the loader again. Then March. A scheduler will fire the exact same job every night, whether or not there is anything new to do.
Two things go wrong if you are naive about the repeat. First, wasted work: if the loader reprocesses January every single time February shows up, your nightly job gets slower and slower as history piles up, re-reading months that have not changed in weeks. Second, and far more dangerous, double-counting: if the loader runs twice for the same month — a retry after a network blip, an accidental double-click, a scheduler that fired twice — January&rsquo;s ~2.96 million rows land …
summary: Append each new month of NYC taxi trips to a SQLite warehouse without reprocessing old months, make re-runs idempotent with a ledger table so nothing is double-counted, and let a crashed load resume where it stopped.
title: Lesson 4 - Incremental & Resumable Pipelines

Welcome to Learned Positional Embeddings In the previous lesson you built sinusoidal positional encoding: a fixed formula of sines and cosines that stamps each position with a unique pattern, no training required. It is elegant, but it is not what GPT actually does. This lesson teaches the approach the real GPT-2 uses instead, and it is almost embarrassingly simple: a learned positional embedding, a plain lookup table of position vectors that the model trains like any other weight.
Our mini-GPT already has a token embedding that maps each character id to a vector. Here you add its twin: a positional table P where row t holds the embedding for position t. To tell the model where each token sits in the sequence, you add these two embeddings together. That sum, token_emb + P[:T], is the input the rest of the transformer will attend over in later modules.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Define a learned positional embedding table P of shape (block_size, C) and explain what …
summary: Build the learned positional embedding table GPT actually uses: a trainable P of shape (block_size, C) you add to token embeddings, with a gradient check.
title: Lesson 4 - Learned Positional Embeddings

Welcome to Calibrating &amp; Trusting the Judge In the last three lessons you taught a model to grade Docent&rsquo;s answers about Meridian — a rubric and direct scores in Lesson 2, pairwise preference in Lesson 3. Every one of those techniques quietly assumed the judge is right. This lesson attacks that assumption head on, and it is the most important lesson in the module: a judge is itself a model, and a model can be confidently, systematically wrong. A judge that scores everything a 4, or always picks the first option, or rewards the longest answer, will hand you a beautiful dashboard full of numbers that mean nothing. Before you let a judge gate a deploy, you have to earn the right to trust it — and &ldquo;earn&rdquo; here means measure.
The tool for that measurement is older than LLMs: treat the judge as a classifier and compare it against a small set of human judgements you trust. If the judge and a human agree on 9 of 10 answers, you can lean on it for the other thousands. If …

Welcome to the Ship Decision You&rsquo;ve built the two-proportion z-test, learned to read the p-value honestly, and wrapped the effect in a confidence interval. Lumen&rsquo;s numbers are settled: the new signup page lifted conversion by +2.20 points, with p = 0.00048 and a 95% CI of [+0.97, +3.43] points. So — do you ship it? The temptation is to glance at the tiny p-value, declare victory, and roll it out. But significance is necessary, not sufficient. A result can be statistically real and still be the wrong thing to ship: too small to justify the cost, or a primary win that quietly broke something else. This lesson turns a test result into a decision using four checks, then walks all four honestly on Lumen — including the part that&rsquo;s genuinely borderline.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Run the four ship-decision checks: significance, practical significance, guardrails, and the confidence interval Compare an observed effect to the MDE you set at design time, …
summary: A significant p-value is necessary but not sufficient — turn Lumen's result into a ship/no-ship call using four checks: significance, the confidence interval, practical significance against the MDE, and guardrails.
title: Lesson 4 - Making the Ship Decision

Welcome to Long-Term Memory with a Vector Store In Lesson 1 you saw the limit clearly: the messages list vanishes when the session ends. Start a new run tomorrow and the agent knows nothing about today — not that the traveler is vegetarian, not that they hate the cold, not what you already worked out together. The fixes from Lessons 2 and 3 keep the current conversation inside the context window, but they do nothing for facts that should outlive a single run. That&rsquo;s what long-term memory is for, and the standard way to build it is a vector store.
The idea is small once you see it. Store each durable fact as a short text note. To recall something, don&rsquo;t try to match exact words — find the notes most relevant to what you need right now by comparing meaning. A vector store does exactly that: it turns each note into a vector (an embedding), turns your query into a vector too, and returns the notes whose vectors are closest. This lesson builds a tiny one you can run with only …
summary: Give your agent memory that survives across sessions — store durable facts as notes in a vector store and retrieve the relevant ones by meaning.
title: Lesson 4 - Long-Term Memory with a Vector Store

Welcome to Common Table Expressions Nested subqueries are powerful, but reading them means working inside-out, mentally unwrapping layer after layer of parentheses. There is a cleaner way. A common table expression (CTE) lets you give a subquery a name and define it up front, then refer to that name in your main query — so your logic reads top to bottom, like a story.
In this lesson you will write single and multiple CTEs with the WITH clause, and then meet recursive CTEs, which can traverse tree-structured data such as a company&rsquo;s reporting hierarchy.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Replace a subquery with a named CTE using the WITH clause Chain multiple CTEs together in one query Apply CTE style conventions for clean, readable SQL Explain the idea of recursion Write a recursive CTE to traverse a hierarchy You should be comfortable with multi-column subqueries from Lesson 2. Let&rsquo;s begin.
Data for this lesson
Database: chinook.db — a digital music store …
summary: Make complex queries readable with WITH, and traverse hierarchies using recursive CTEs.
title: Lesson 4 - Common Table Expressions (CTEs)

Welcome to Middleware and CORS So far, every piece of logic you&rsquo;ve written lives inside one endpoint. But some jobs aren&rsquo;t about a single route — they&rsquo;re about every route. You might want to time how long each request takes, stamp a header on every response, or log who&rsquo;s calling. Copy-pasting that into all your endpoints would be exactly the duplication you&rsquo;ve been learning to avoid. The tool for these whole-app jobs is middleware: a layer that wraps every request on its way in and every response on its way out.
In this lesson you&rsquo;ll write your own middleware, then meet a built-in one that solves a problem you&rsquo;ll hit the moment a web page tries to call your API: CORS. Browsers block cross-origin requests by default, and CORS is how your API tells the browser which sites it trusts.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Explain what middleware is and why it runs on every request Write custom HTTP middleware that times requests and adds …

title: Lesson 4 - Middleware and CORS

Welcome to Repository Anatomy Your SkyLog repository is online now, and your commits are safely pushed. But if a stranger landed on its GitHub page right now, would they understand what it does, how to run it, or whether they&rsquo;re even allowed to use it? Probably not. A repository that&rsquo;s only code is like a book with no cover, no blurb, and no copyright page — useful to the author, baffling to everyone else.
This lesson is less about typing commands and more about the few small files and settings that turn a pile of code into a project people can actually understand and use. You&rsquo;ll meet the three files that almost every good repository has — a README, a LICENSE, and a .gitignore — and the GitHub touches that make a project discoverable: a clear description and a handful of topics.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Write a README that explains what your project is, why it exists, and how to run it Explain what a LICENSE is and why a repo without one …
summary: Make your repository clear and usable: a strong README, a LICENSE, a clean .gitignore, and a good GitHub description and topics.

Welcome to the Naive Bayes Algorithm In the last lessons you learned Bayes&rsquo; theorem as a rule for updating a single belief when one piece of evidence arrives. Now you will turn that rule into something that does real work: a classifier — a program that reads a piece of text and decides which category it belongs to.
The category here is a familiar annoyance. Some news headlines are honest summaries; others are clickbait, engineered to make you click without telling you anything (&ldquo;You Won&rsquo;t Believe What Happened Next&rdquo;). You will build the algorithm that separates the two, using nothing but counts of words and the theorem you already know. It is called Naive Bayes, and despite the dismissive name it is one of the most effective, most widely used text classifiers ever written.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Frame classification as comparing P(clickbait∣words) P(\text{clickbait} \mid \text{words}) against P(genuine∣words) P(\text{genuine} \mid …

title: Lesson 4 - The Naive Bayes Algorithm

What if you have a query you run constantly, and you want to save it permanently so anyone can use it without rewriting it? In this lesson you will create views, query them, build views on top of other views, and learn how to drop them safely.

content:
Welcome to the Guided Project Across this module you learned each piece on its own: what GitHub is, how to register a remote, how to push, and how to keep local and remote in sync. Now you&rsquo;ll put it all together in one continuous run. Starting from your local SkyLog repository — the small project you&rsquo;ve been building, with its commits and README already in place — you&rsquo;ll take it from &ldquo;lives only on my laptop&rdquo; to &ldquo;online, backed up, and shareable&rdquo; in a single sitting.

Create an empty repository on GitHub using the web interface or the gh CLI Connect your local repo to that remote and publish it with a first push Confirm your files and README render correctly on the GitHub repo …

content:
Welcome to the Guided Project Every lesson in this module fixed one problem at a time. This project combines all of them into a single function, clean_orders(), run once against the full thistlewood_orders_raw.csv — and then proves it worked by checking the result against real canonical Thistlewood data, not just by running the data-quality report from Lesson 5.

content:

content:

Start with Lesson 1, where every scattered AppTest check this course has run becomes one real, …

content:
Every model built through Module 4 sat in one of two layers: staging, a thin rename-only pass over a source, or a mart that happened to also do the aggregating. This module names the layer in between precisely, and gives CityFlow real dimension and fact models for the first time — checked against dbt Labs&rsquo; current documentation, which has moved on from what this course&rsquo;s blueprint originally assumed.
CityFlow already has an intermediate model — int_hourly_pattern, built back in Module 2 — and this module opens by explaining what makes it intermediate rather than staging or mart, before building zones and trips: a real dimension enriched with a computed is_airport flag, and a real fact table joining against it — the first join this project has run in a mart layer, where Module 4&rsquo;s rule says a join actually belongs. The module closes with this Data Engineering path&rsquo;s recurring anchor, reproduced as a dbt model for the first time: the same zone-hour report the …
summary: Why intermediate models exist as a layer, star-schema thinking applied to CityFlow's zones and trips, a real zone dimension and trip fact model, and a guided project reproducing this path's own anchor figures -- 240,917 buckets, 9,554,757 trips, $256,692,373.14 -- as a dbt model, …

content:
Module 4&rsquo;s own guided project ran into something this module explains properly: a real KRaft controller leader election happened mid-run on this course&rsquo;s own cluster, and a handful of produced messages were silently lost until real error handling caught it. This module goes inside the mechanism that caused that — how brokers register with the controller and stay alive via heartbeats, how a partition&rsquo;s leader, replicas, and in-sync-replica set actually work together, and what a produce or fetch request does once it reaches a broker.
Then it stops being theoretical. This module&rsquo;s hands-on lab stops a real broker — docker stop kafka2 — while producing to a real topic, and watches, with real command output at every step, exactly what a distributed system built for this is supposed to do: the in-sync replica set shrinks, leadership moves to a broker that&rsquo;s still healthy, writes with acks='all' keep succeeding the whole time as long as enough replicas remain, …
summary: See how brokers actually find each other and agree on metadata in KRaft, build the real mental model behind leaders/replicas/ISR, trace the produce and fetch path, then kill a real broker mid-produce and watch the cluster recover.
title: Kafka Internals: Replication, Leaders, and Failure

content:
Every table this course has worked with so far has been flat — one row, one order, one product, columns that hold a single value each. Real-world data isn&rsquo;t always shaped that way: an API response, an export from another system, or a document database often nests related data together, one order with its line items bundled right inside it. This module works with exactly that shape: a real nested JSON export of Thistlewood Goods&rsquo; Q1 2024 orders, each one carrying its own list of line items directly inside the record.
You&rsquo;ll read that file directly with read_json_auto, which does something CSV reading never had to: infer a genuinely nested schema, typing line_items as a real list of structs rather than a flat column. From there you&rsquo;ll query into that nested structure with plain SQL — dot notation for struct fields, bracket indexing for list elements — flatten it into a normal one-row-per-line-item table with UNNEST, and write results back out to JSON in both array …
summary: Read JSON files directly into typed structs and lists, query nested data with SQL, flatten it into normal tables, and write results back out to JSON.
title: Working with JSON and Nested Data

content:
Module 4 cleaned Thistlewood&rsquo;s order data. This module turns to the product catalog, and the messiness looks different: not nulls or bad numbers, but text that says the right thing in the wrong shape. thistlewood_products_raw.csv, a 61-row variant of the canonical 60-row thistlewood_products.csv, arrives with 14 rows whose category uses inconsistent capitalization or trailing whitespace (&quot;kitchen&quot;, &quot;KITCHEN&quot;, &quot;Bath &quot;), 6 rows whose product_name has extra whitespace or the wrong casing, and one extra row entirely &ndash; an existing product re-entered under a slightly respelled name. Every one of these counts is accurate and reproducible, built by a seeded generator script the same way every other Thistlewood messiness variant in this course was built.
Lesson 1 opens the string namespace directly: .str.strip_chars(), .str.to_lowercase()/.str.to_uppercase(), and .str.len_chars(), run against the messy rows to see exactly what each one does and does not …
summary: Clean a messy Thistlewood product catalog -- strip and case-normalize text with the string namespace, extract and replace values with regex, collapse a 22-string category mess down to 8 canonical categories, and use pl.Categorical/pl.Enum.
title: Strings, Categories, and Text Workflows

content:
Welcome to Orchestrating ETL, Module 5 of Orchestrating Data Pipelines with Airflow. Every DAG so far has been a learning exercise — small, deliberately scoped to one idea at a time. This module is where that changes: you&rsquo;ll rebuild CityFlow&rsquo;s real pipeline as a DAG shaped the way a production ETL job actually looks, and run it against real data at a scale this course hasn&rsquo;t used before.
The shape is ingest → validate → transform → load, and Lesson 1 doesn&rsquo;t just name that shape — it shows why the boundaries sit exactly there, with a real DAG run that fails on purpose partway through to prove a validation failure stops the pipeline before any transform work is wasted. Lessons 2 through 4 build each stage: ingest reads a genuine slice of CityFlow&rsquo;s actual January 2024 taxi data straight off a ~50MB parquet file, validate runs five genuine data-quality checks and writes its findings to a real JSON report and a real quarantine CSV instead of just printing a …
summary: CityFlow's real pipeline, rebuilt as a production-shaped Airflow DAG: dedicated ingest, validate, transform, and load tasks, real data-quality checks with inspectable results, and a real three-day slice of NYC taxi data loaded into Postgres.
title: Orchestrating ETL

content:
Welcome to Kubernetes Concepts on Kind, the fifth module of Docker &amp; Kubernetes for Data Engineering. Modules 1 through 4 gave CityFlow&rsquo;s pipeline everything Docker alone can offer: images, your own Dockerfiles, and a Compose file that starts a whole stack with one command, on one machine. This module answers the question Compose can&rsquo;t: what happens when &ldquo;one machine&rdquo; isn&rsquo;t enough — when a container needs to be rescheduled onto a different machine after a failure, or a fleet of services needs a control plane deciding where each one runs? That&rsquo;s Kubernetes, and every example in this module runs on a real, already-running local cluster: Kind (Kubernetes in Docker).
You&rsquo;ll start by proving, literally, that Kind is not a separate piece of infrastructure — it&rsquo;s Kubernetes&rsquo; entire control plane running as containers inside one Docker container you already know how to inspect. From there you&rsquo;ll run your first real pod by hand and …
summary: A real local Kubernetes cluster, built from Docker containers: pods, self-healing Deployments, Services, Namespaces, and the Dashboard.
title: Kubernetes Concepts on Kind

content:
Welcome to Handing the Loop Over. So far you&rsquo;ve run every loop yourself, one message at a time. This module hands the loop to an agent that runs the whole cycle on its own — attempt, check, correct, repeat — over the real files on your computer. The tools are Claude Code and Codex, and the most important thing to say up front is that they are not just for developers. They are file agents: point one at a folder of messy documents and it will read, sort, rename, and summarize them for you. A non-developer doing exactly that is doing real loop engineering.
You&rsquo;ll start by understanding what an agentic command-line tool actually is, in plain terms, and why the &ldquo;it&rsquo;s for coders&rdquo; label sells it short. Then, before you let anything run on its own, you&rsquo;ll learn safety and permissions — the single most important idea in the module: the rules you write shape what the agent tries to do, but a separate layer decides what it&rsquo;s allowed to do. Writing …
summary: Agentic file tools aren't just for developers. Learn to set one up safely, run your first autonomous loop, give it a way to check itself, and use project memory.
title: Handing the Loop Over: Claude Code and Codex for Everyone

content:
Welcome to Partitions, Shuffles &amp; Caching, the fifth module — where Spark tuning stops being about the query and starts being about the machine underneath it. Module 4 ended on the one thing it could not optimize away: the group-by&rsquo;s Exchange, the shuffle that aggregating by key genuinely requires. It left you with a sharper question than &ldquo;how do I avoid this shuffle?&rdquo; — namely, &ldquo;how big is it, and can I make it cheaper?&rdquo; That question is where real Spark performance lives, and answering it means understanding the three levers this module is named for.
The first is the partition — the unit of parallelism, one task per partition. How many partitions your data is split into decides how many cores can work at once, how much scheduling overhead you pay, and how big each shuffle piece is; you&rsquo;ll learn to see the count, control it with repartition and coalesce, and recognize when there are too few or too many. The second is the shuffle itself — the …
summary: Where Spark performance actually lives. Learn what a partition is and how many the data wants, why the shuffle is the most expensive thing Spark does and how to make it cheaper, when caching a DataFrame pays and when it just wastes memory, and how a single hot key like JFK turns …
title: Partitions, Shuffles & Caching

content:
Welcome to Parallel Processing, the fifth module — where your pipeline stops using one CPU core and starts using all of them. Everything so far ran on a single core: correct, memory-lean, but leaving most of your machine idle. A modern laptop has eight or ten cores; a data-engineering job that ignores them is running at a fraction of its potential.
This module is honest about when parallelism helps. You&rsquo;ll learn why Python&rsquo;s Global Interpreter Lock means threads give almost no speedup for CPU-bound work, while separate processes genuinely run in parallel. You&rsquo;ll drive a multiprocessing Pool, structure work as map-reduce (compute partial results per partition, then combine them), and sidestep the biggest trap — the cost of serializing large data to workers — by having each worker read its own partition. Along the way you&rsquo;ll measure everything, because the speedup is never the number of cores: it plateaus, exactly as Amdahl&rsquo;s law predicts.
Start with Lesson …
summary: Use every CPU core to speed up data work — and measure the real gain. Understand the GIL and why data pipelines use processes not threads, drive a multiprocessing Pool, apply the map-reduce pattern, process partitions in parallel without paying serialization costs, and watch …
title: Parallel Processing

content:
Welcome to The Transformer Block, the fifth module. You&rsquo;ve built attention; now you&rsquo;ll build everything around it that turns a single clever operation into a deep, trainable network. A transformer is just this block, repeated — so getting it right is what makes the whole model work.
You&rsquo;ll add the three ingredients that make depth possible. Residual connections give gradients a direct path backward, so a twenty-layer stack trains as easily as a two-layer one. Layer normalization keeps each position&rsquo;s activations well-scaled from block to block — and you&rsquo;ll derive its famously subtle backward pass and gradient-check it. The feed-forward network, a small position-wise MLP that expands and contracts the representation, gives each position room to compute. Then you&rsquo;ll assemble all of it — multi-head attention from Module 3, layer norm, the feed-forward network, and residual connections — into the pre-norm transformer block, verify it end to end, and …
summary: Attention alone doesn't make a transformer. Learn the three pieces that make deep stacks trainable — residual connections, layer normalization, and the position-wise feed-forward network — then assemble them with multi-head attention into the repeatable transformer block, forward …
title: The Transformer Block

content:
Welcome to Evaluating RAG, the fifth module. Docent is a retrieval-augmented system: it retrieves the Meridian doc pages most relevant to a question, then generates an answer from them. That means a wrong answer has two possible causes — the retriever fed the model the wrong context, or the model mishandled the right context — and if you only measure the final answer, you can&rsquo;t tell which. This module teaches you to evaluate both halves.
You&rsquo;ll learn retrieval metrics — precision, recall, MRR, and NDCG — to score whether the right documents came back, then faithfulness and groundedness to catch a generator that invents claims the context doesn&rsquo;t support, and finally answer relevance and context quality to judge the pipeline as a whole. Along the way you&rsquo;ll reconnect with a bug you met in Module 1: Docent&rsquo;s keyword retriever quietly pulls the wrong pages for certain questions. The guided project runs a full RAG evaluation on Docent and, crucially, diagnoses …
summary: A RAG system is two systems in one — a retriever and a generator — and each fails differently. Learn retrieval metrics, faithfulness and groundedness, answer relevance and context quality, then run a full RAG evaluation on Docent that pinpoints where failures come from.
title: Evaluating RAG

content:
Welcome to the Capstone, the final stop in the Gradient Boosting &amp; XGBoost course. Every module ended with a guided project. This one is different: it takes a single real dataset — Adult Income — from raw data all the way to a tuned, explained, honestly evaluated model, using skills from all four modules at once.
You&rsquo;ll explore and prepare the data, handle its genuine class imbalance and categorical features with XGBoost&rsquo;s native tools, train with early stopping and cross-validation, tune systematically with Optuna, explain the finished model with SHAP, and report metrics honestly with the precision/recall trade-offs stated plainly. A final report traces every step back to the module that taught it.
Every number in this capstone comes from real, executed code. Start the lesson to build one complete, trustworthy model end to end.
summary: One final end-to-end build: take the Adult Income dataset from raw data to a tuned, explained, honestly evaluated XGBoost model using every skill from all four modules.

content:
Welcome to the Capstone, the final stop in the Software Engineering Fundamentals course. Every module so far has ended with its own guided project. This one is different: it pulls all four modules together into a single, real feature for Ledgerly — prorated mid-cycle subscription plan upgrades — built completely from scratch.
You&rsquo;ll frame the work with user stories and a methodology choice from Engineering Foundations, design a composed ProrationCalculator with a deliberately chosen pattern from Design, Architecture &amp; OOP, implement and thoroughly test it using the practices from Writing Quality, Tested Code, and close with the CI and security awareness from Delivery &amp; Operations.
