This module names the templating language directly: what {{ }} and {% %} each do, why they compile to different things, and what dbt&rsquo;s compiler produces from each — checked against target/compiled/, not assumed.
Control flow gets built by hand next: a {% for %} loop pivots CityFlow&rsquo;s trip counts across its boroughs into columns, and a {% if %} block changes what SQL actually compiles depending on a condition — the same mechanism {{ config(enabled = target.type == 'duckdb') }} from Module 5 already used. Two genuinely duplicated expressions already sitting in CityFlow&rsquo;s models — one repeated date_trunc call, one repeated rounding pattern — become the motivation for writing macros, before turning to dbt_utils&rsquo;s own macro library: date_spine, …
summary: What dbt actually compiles before a query reaches Postgres: Jinja's {{ }} vs {% %}, control flow inside a CityFlow model, a hand-written macro replacing duplicated SQL, dbt_utils's macro library, and a guided project that DRYs up CityFlow's marts.
title: Jinja and Macros

content:
Module 5 explained how a Kafka cluster survives a broker failure without losing availability. This module asks the next question: under all of that machinery, what exactly does Kafka promise about whether your data survives, and what do you have to configure — on the producer, the broker, and the consumer — to actually get that promise instead of just assuming it?
The answer starts with a genuinely crashed process, not a diagram. This module kills a real consumer with SIGKILL mid-run, once with the offset committed before processing and once with it committed after, and reads back exactly what &ldquo;at-most-once&rdquo; and &ldquo;at-least-once&rdquo; mean from the resulting gap or duplicate — not from a definition alone. From there it moves broker-side, comparing a replication-factor-1 topic against a replication-factor-3 topic during a real outage, and confronting a genuine limit of this course&rsquo;s own 3-broker lab cluster along the way. Then it introduces confluent-kafka, the …
summary: Define at-most-once, at-least-once, and exactly-once precisely and prove each one with a real crashed process, configure the broker-side settings that actually enforce reliability, use confluent-kafka's idempotent and transactional producers to eliminate duplicate-on-retry for …
title: Reliable Data Delivery

content:
Module 2 built the SQL foundation this course leans on — filtering, sorting, GROUP BY, joins. GROUP BY has a real limit, though: it collapses rows down to one per group, which is exactly wrong when the question is &ldquo;rank these without losing any of them&rdquo; or &ldquo;show a running total alongside every individual value.&rdquo; This module covers the SQL built specifically for that: window functions, which compute across a set of rows without collapsing them.
You&rsquo;ll rank and compare rows with ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and DENSE_RANK — including a real, genuine tie in the data that makes the difference between them concrete rather than theoretical. You&rsquo;ll build running totals and moving averages with window frames, reshape data between wide and long form with DuckDB&rsquo;s native PIVOT and UNPIVOT, and work with dates and times — extracting parts, doing date arithmetic, and formatting output. The module closes with a guided project that combines all four into one sales …
summary: Window functions, running totals and moving averages, PIVOT/UNPIVOT, and date/time functions -- the SQL analytics actually runs on, taught hands-on.
title: Advanced SQL for Analytics

content:
Every Thistlewood table so far has been flat: one row, one order or one product, every value a single scalar in its own column. Real-world data doesn&rsquo;t always arrive that way. A JSON export from an e-commerce API is a common example: instead of a separate order_items table joined by order_id, each order record embeds its own line items directly, as a list nested inside that one row. This module builds a file shaped exactly that way &ndash; thistlewood_orders_nested.json &ndash; and teaches the tools Polars gives you for working with a column whose values aren&rsquo;t scalars at all.
thistlewood_orders_nested.json is a deterministic re-shaping of Thistlewood&rsquo;s own canonical order data &ndash; no invented values, no random draw. It covers the same Q1 2024 quarter (2024-01-01 through 2024-03-31) Module 4&rsquo;s thistlewood_orders_raw.csv already used, and for the same reason: a manageable subset rather than the full two-year, 6,000-order history. Each of its 792 order records …
summary: Build and work with a nested Thistlewood dataset -- pl.List vs pl.Array, list.eval() transformations, pl.struct() for grouped values, and an explode()-based flatten verified row-for-row against the flat source.
title: Work with Nested Data

content:
Welcome to Testing, Logging &amp; Monitoring DAGs, Module 6 of Orchestrating Data Pipelines with Airflow. cityflow_etl_dag.py works — Module 5 proved that with a real ~239,000-row run, a Postgres load, and a screenshot of four green boxes. Working isn&rsquo;t the same as trustworthy. Nobody watches this DAG live at 3 a.m., so the pipeline itself has to be able to prove its own logic is correct, tell you exactly what happened when it breaks, show you where the time went, and say something the instant it fails. That&rsquo;s this module.
Lesson 1 pulls validate_trips&rsquo;s five real data-quality checks out into a plain, importable function and unit-tests it in total isolation — no scheduler, no worker, not even Airflow installed — and measures the real difference: a real test suite finishing in 200 milliseconds against a real DAG-trigger-and-poll cycle that took 6.68 seconds for a three-task DAG doing almost nothing. Lesson 2 goes past the happy-path log tour Module 2 already gave you: …
summary: Making CityFlow's ETL DAG trustworthy, not just runnable: real unit tests for task logic outside the scheduler, reading a real failed task's log, the Grid and Gantt views for a real multi-task run, a real on_failure_callback, and a guided project that instruments Module 5's ETL …
title: Testing, Logging & Monitoring DAGs

content:
Welcome to Config, Storage and Batch Jobs, the sixth module of Docker &amp; Kubernetes for Data Engineering. Module 5 gave CityFlow a real service running on Kubernetes — a Deployment and a Service, self-healing and reachable by name. But that service had everything hardcoded into its image, stored nothing that survived a pod being deleted, and only knew how to run forever. This module fills in every one of those gaps with the pieces a real data pipeline actually needs.
You&rsquo;ll start by externalizing a service&rsquo;s configuration two different ways — a ConfigMap for its ordinary settings, and a Secret for anything sensitive, with a close look at exactly why kubectl get secret -o yaml shows base64 rather than the real value, and why that is not encryption on its own. From there you&rsquo;ll give Kubernetes its own answer to Module 4&rsquo;s Docker volume: a PersistentVolumeClaim whose data survives a pod being deleted and recreated, backed by the StorageClass this cluster already …
summary: Externalized config, durable storage, and real run-to-completion Jobs and CronJobs — the pieces a Kubernetes data pipeline actually needs.
title: Config, Storage and Batch Jobs

content:
Welcome to Designing Loops That Stop. In Module 1 you learned that every loop needs a place to stop; now you&rsquo;ll learn to design that stop deliberately. This is the safety and cost module, and its blunt version is this: a loop that can&rsquo;t stop isn&rsquo;t a tool, it&rsquo;s a bill. An agent that keeps working past the point of usefulness wastes money, produces worse output, and can take actions you didn&rsquo;t want — so knowing how a loop ends is as important as knowing how it starts.
You&rsquo;ll learn the real stop conditions a loop can hit: it finished successfully, it hit a budget you set, or it decided to give up. You&rsquo;ll set budgets in the units that matter — number of turns, wall-clock time, and money — and learn where each kind of limit belongs. You&rsquo;ll learn to spot a stuck loop: one that&rsquo;s thrashing between two versions, oscillating, or slowly drifting away from the goal. You&rsquo;ll teach a loop to escalate — to stop and ask you a question instead …
summary: A loop that can't stop is a bill, not a tool. Learn stop conditions, budgets, spotting a stuck loop, teaching a loop to ask, and reading its trace.
title: Designing Loops That Stop

content:
Welcome to Building ETL Pipelines in Spark, the sixth module — where everything you&rsquo;ve learned about the engine turns into a job you can hand to a scheduler. The first five modules made you fluent: you understand how Spark thinks, you can write the DataFrame API and Spark SQL, you can read a plan and tune the physical execution. But every query so far has been something you ran — typed at a session, watched, verified. Production data engineering is different. It is a job that runs tonight at 2 a.m. with nobody watching, reads whatever the source dropped that day, cleans it, transforms it, and writes a result other systems depend on — and does the same thing correctly every night, including the night the source data arrives a little wrong or the job gets retried after a failure. This module is about building that job.
Four disciplines separate a production ETL from an ad-hoc query, and each is a lesson. The first is the schema: production code declares the shape of its data …
summary: Turn ad-hoc queries into a production job. Declare an explicit schema instead of inferring one, structure the read-clean-transform body as tested functions that preserve the data's real defects, write a partitioned Parquet analytics table, and make the whole job idempotent so a …
title: Building ETL Pipelines in Spark

content:
Welcome to Data Structures for Data Work, the sixth module — where your pipeline stops doing work it never needed to do. Module 5 spread the job across every core on the machine and cut the wall clock by nearly four. That is a real win, but it is also a blunt one: parallelism makes slow code finish sooner without making it less wasteful. If every trip triggers a linear scan through a list of zones to find a borough name, six processes just perform that wasteful scan six times at once. The deeper fix is to change the shape of the data so the scan never happens.
That is what a data structure buys you. A dict finds a zone by id in the same time whether it holds ten entries or ten million, because hashing jumps straight to the answer instead of looking through the candidates. A set answers &ldquo;have I seen this trip before?&rdquo; the same way. A deque gives a streaming buffer a genuinely constant-time front, where a plain list quietly re-copies every element on each pop(0). A heap hands …
summary: The right data structure makes the access pattern cheap. Learn why a dict finds a zone instantly while a list hunts for it, why popping the front of a list is a hidden trap and a deque is not, how a heap answers top-N without sorting anything, and how to choose between them by …
title: Data Structures for Data Work

content:
Welcome to Causal Masking &amp; GPT, the sixth module — where all the parts click together into a real language model. You have attention, multi-head attention, positional embeddings, and the transformer block. The one thing standing between that and a GPT is a rule about time: to predict the next token, a position must never be allowed to peek at the tokens that come after it.
You&rsquo;ll start with the autoregressive idea — that language modeling is just next-token prediction, done at every position in parallel. Then you&rsquo;ll implement the causal mask that enforces it, setting the attention scores above the diagonal to negative infinity so each position attends only to itself and the past. You&rsquo;ll stack causal transformer blocks into the decoder-only architecture that GPT uses, and add the language-modeling head — a projection to vocabulary logits — with the softmax cross-entropy next-token loss whose gradient you&rsquo;ll derive and check. The guided project assembles the …
summary: Turn the transformer block into a GPT: the autoregressive next-token objective, the causal mask that stops a position from seeing the future, the decoder-only stack, and the language-modeling head and loss — assembling a complete mini-GPT in NumPy, forward and backward.
title: Causal Masking & GPT

content:
Welcome to Evaluating Agents &amp; Tool Use, the sixth module. So far Docent has answered in a single pass. But a real assistant is often an agent: it decides for itself to search the docs, reads what comes back, maybe searches again, and only then answers. That autonomy adds an entire new surface to evaluate — the path the agent takes — and a wrong answer can now hide a wrong tool, wrong arguments, a redundant loop, or a premature give-up that a final-answer check would never reveal.
You&rsquo;ll learn to evaluate agents at three levels: task success (did it actually accomplish the goal?), tool-call correctness (did it call the right tool with valid arguments?), and trajectory evaluation (was the sequence of steps efficient and sound, or did it wander?). Each answers a different question, and you need all three: an agent can reach the right answer by a terrible path, or take a perfect path to the wrong place. The guided project turns Docent into a tool-using agent and evaluates it end …
summary: An agent doesn't just produce an answer — it takes a path of tool calls to get there, and that path can fail in ways a final-answer check never sees. Learn task success, tool-call correctness, and trajectory evaluation, then evaluate an agentic Docent end to end.
title: Evaluating Agents & Tool Use

content:
Welcome to Seasonality: SARIMA, the sixth module of the course. Module 5 reached an honest wall: a non-seasonal ARIMA, no matter how carefully tuned, couldn&rsquo;t cleanly beat the simple seasonal-naive baseline on Cyclepath — the best stable model managed 16% MAPE against the baseline&rsquo;s 5.9%, because ARIMA has no term whose job is to capture &ldquo;this July resembles last July.&rdquo; SARIMA fixes exactly that gap, and this module is where the whole course pays off.
You&rsquo;ll start by extending ARIMA to SARIMA — adding a second set of orders (P, D, Q)[s] that operate at the seasonal lag, alongside the familiar non-seasonal (p, d, q). You&rsquo;ll build the seasonal AR and MA terms and see how a seasonal-AR coefficient relates this period to the same period a full cycle ago. You&rsquo;ll fit a SARIMA to Cyclepath with statsmodels, reading the summary and forecasting. You&rsquo;ll run proper diagnostics — the Ljung-Box residual test that Module 4&rsquo;s preview model failed …
summary: Extend ARIMA with seasonal terms — a second (P, D, Q) applied at the seasonal lag — to model the yearly structure that non-seasonal ARIMA couldn't, and finally beat the seasonal-naive baseline on Cyclepath.
title: Seasonality: SARIMA

content:
Welcome to Pitfalls and Validity, the sixth module. So far you&rsquo;ve learned to design, size, and analyze experiments correctly. But here&rsquo;s the uncomfortable truth: you can run every calculation perfectly and still reach a confidently wrong conclusion. The failures in this module don&rsquo;t come from bad arithmetic — they come from how the test was run and read: checking the results too often, testing too many things, slicing the data the wrong way, or missing that the experiment was broken from the start. These are the mistakes that survive peer review and ship bad decisions, because the p-value looks fine.
You&rsquo;ll see each trap manufactured in simulation, so you believe it. Peeking: stopping the moment a test crosses significance turns a 5% false-positive rate into nearly 20%. Multiple comparisons: testing 20 metrics gives you a 64% chance of a &ldquo;winner&rdquo; that&rsquo;s pure noise — and how a Bonferroni correction fixes it. Simpson&rsquo;s paradox: a treatment …
summary: The traps that make a correctly-run test lie — peeking, multiple comparisons, Simpson's paradox, and a broken split — and the sanity checks that catch them before you trust a result.
title: Pitfalls and Validity

content:
Welcome to Retrieval-Augmented Agents, the sixth module. Your agent can loop, use tools, remember, and plan — but it still answers from a fixed pool of training knowledge that can&rsquo;t see your documents, your latest data, or anything private. When it doesn&rsquo;t know, it tends to guess confidently. This module fixes that by giving the agent retrieval: the ability to look things up in a knowledge base you control, and to ground its answers in what it finds.
You&rsquo;ll start with why agents need retrieval — grounding, fresh and private knowledge, and fewer confident wrong answers. You&rsquo;ll build a knowledge base: chunk documents into passages, embed them, and search by similarity. You&rsquo;ll then expose retrieval as a tool so the agent decides when to look something up, mid-loop — agentic RAG. And you&rsquo;ll add the discipline that makes retrieval trustworthy: grounding and citations — answer only from retrieved sources, cite them, and refuse honestly when the knowledge …
summary: Ground your agent in your own data — build a searchable knowledge base, give the agent a retrieval tool, and make it answer from sources with citations instead of guessing.
title: Retrieval-Augmented Agents

content:
Welcome to Team Workflows, the sixth module of the course. You now know the mechanics of branches, remotes, and pull requests — but working on a team is less about new commands and more about shared conventions. When several people push to the same repository every day, the difference between a smooth project and a chaotic one comes down to agreements: which branches exist and why, what a good commit message looks like, how you stay out of each other&rsquo;s way, and how a finished version becomes a labeled release.
You&rsquo;ll start by comparing branching strategies — GitHub Flow, Git Flow, and trunk-based development — and learn which fits which kind of team. Then you&rsquo;ll adopt Conventional Commits, a simple format that makes history readable and even automatable. You&rsquo;ll pick up the habits that let people work together without stepping on each other, and you&rsquo;ll learn tags and releases with semantic versioning so every shipped version has a name you can return to. …
summary: Work the way professional teams do — choose a branching strategy, write disciplined commit messages, avoid stepping on each other, and ship versioned releases with tags.
title: Team Workflows

content:
Welcome to Authentication and Security, the sixth module of the course. Right now anyone can read, change, or delete every task in your API — there&rsquo;s no notion of who is making a request. Real applications need authentication (knowing who you are) and authorization (knowing what you&rsquo;re allowed to do). This module adds both, using the patterns that have become the industry standard for APIs.
You&rsquo;ll start with the OAuth2 password flow — the login-with-username-and-password pattern FastAPI supports out of the box — and the /token endpoint that powers it. You&rsquo;ll hash passwords so they&rsquo;re never stored in plain text, issue and verify JWT access tokens (signed, tamper-proof, and self-expiring), and write a current-user dependency that turns a token back into a user. Finally you&rsquo;ll protect routes so only logged-in users can reach them, and add role checks so only admins can do admin things. The module ends with a guided project: an auth-protected API where …
summary: Protect your API: log users in with the OAuth2 password flow, hash passwords safely, issue and verify JWT tokens, and gate endpoints behind authentication and roles.
title: Authentication and Security

content:
Welcome to Querying Databases from Python — the module where two of the most important skills in data work finally meet. You already know how to write SQL to ask a database questions, and you have seen how Python lets you clean, reshape, and visualize data. Here you connect the two so that a single Python script can reach into a database, pull back exactly the rows you need, and hand them straight to your analysis tools.
Data for this module
Databases: jobs.db — U.S. recent-graduate job statistics (from FiveThirtyEight), and world_population.db — country population data (both SQLite).
Download the one each lesson needs and place it in your working directory. Each lesson lists the specific table it uses.
You will work with the lightweight sqlite3 library that ships with Python, so there is nothing to install. You will open a connection to a database file, create a cursor to run queries, and learn how SQLite returns each row as a tuple. From there you will move up a level and load query …
summary: Bring SQL into your Python workflow — connect to a database, run queries with sqlite3, and load results into pandas.
title: Querying Databases from Python

content:
Welcome to Vector Databases, the sixth module of the Generative AI &amp; LLM Engineering course. In Module 5 you built a semantic search engine by embedding a handful of documents and comparing every one of them to each query. That works beautifully for fifteen FAQs — but what happens at fifteen thousand, or fifteen million? Re-embedding and re-scanning everything on every query is too slow and wastes memory. A vector database solves this: it stores your embeddings, indexes them for fast nearest-neighbor search, and lets you filter by metadata — all while persisting to disk so you embed your data once and query it forever.
You&rsquo;ll start with why a dedicated store is needed and what an index actually buys you. Then you&rsquo;ll get started with Chroma, an open-source vector database that runs locally and for free — creating a collection, adding documents, and querying by meaning in just a few lines. You&rsquo;ll add metadata and filtering so you can search within a category, and …
summary: Store and search embeddings at scale — why brute-force search breaks down, how a vector database fixes it, and how to build a persistent, filterable search index with Chroma.
title: Vector Databases

content:
Welcome to Pandas Data Analysis—the module that transforms you from a NumPy user into a professional data analyst! Pandas builds on NumPy to provide powerful, labeled data structures that make working with real-world datasets intuitive and efficient.
If NumPy is the engine, pandas is the complete vehicle. You will learn to clean messy data, filter rows based on complex conditions, group and aggregate information, and combine multiple datasets—the core skills every data analyst uses daily.
summary: Master pandas for professional data manipulation and analysis with Python
title: Pandas Data Analysis

content:
Welcome to Matplotlib and Seaborn with st.pyplot Module 3 covered three charting approaches — Streamlit&rsquo;s built-ins, Plotly, Altair — and never touched the library most real analysis work is actually built on. This lesson bridges that gap: st.pyplot, and the one real gotcha every matplotlib-in-Streamlit app needs to know.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Render a real matplotlib or seaborn figure in Streamlit with st.pyplot Explain why AppTest can confirm a figure exists but not what it actually shows Confirm, with a real figure count, why plt.close(fig) matters in a Streamlit app A Real Seaborn Boxplot import pathlib import urllib.request if not pathlib.Path(&#34;gapminder.csv&#34;).exists(): request = urllib.request.Request( &#34;https://datatweets.com/datasets/gapminder.csv&#34;, headers={&#34;User-Agent&#34;: &#34;Mozilla/5.0&#34;}, ) with urllib.request.urlopen(request) as response, open(&#34;gapminder.csv&#34;, &#34;wb&#34;) as f: f.write(response.read()) …
summary: A real seaborn boxplot -- 2007 life expectancy by continent, showing Africa's real, wide spread against Oceania's near-flat one -- rendered with st.pyplot, plus a genuine, confirmed memory-leak gotcha: every Streamlit rerun creates a new matplotlib figure, and plt.close(fig) is …
title: Lesson 1 - Matplotlib and Seaborn with st.pyplot

content:
Welcome to Jinja in SQL Every .sql file this project has written since Module 1 looked like SQL — but {{ ref('stg_cityflow__trips') }}, {{ source('cityflow', 'zones') }}, and Module 5&rsquo;s {{ config(enabled = target.type == 'duckdb') }} were never SQL at all. They&rsquo;re Jinja, a Python templating library dbt runs over every model before a single query reaches Postgres or DuckDB — the same templating engine Flask uses to render HTML, borrowed by dbt to render SQL instead, with the warehouse standing in for the browser. This lesson names it directly and shows exactly what it compiles to.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Tell {{ }} and {% %} apart by what each one compiles to, not just by convention Use dbt compile --inline to inspect compiled SQL without writing a model file Explain why swapping {{ }} and {% %} produces a compile error, not a warning What {{ }} and {% %} Each Compile To {{ expression }} outputs a value into the compiled SQL -- ref(), source(), a …
summary: Every model built through Module 5 already used Jinja without naming it. This lesson names {{ }} and {% %} directly, and uses dbt compile --inline to watch each one compile to something different -- one substitutes the literal value it evaluates to, the other sets state and …
title: Lesson 1 - Jinja in SQL

content:
Welcome to Reliable Data Delivery Module 4 Lesson 2 introduced manual offset commits and warned that when you commit relative to when you process changes what happens if the consumer dies at the wrong moment. This lesson stops treating that as a warning and turns it into three precisely defined guarantees, two of which get proven here with a real process killed by SIGKILL — the same uncatchable, no-cleanup signal a real crash or kill -9 sends.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Define at-most-once, at-least-once, and exactly-once precisely, not just by name Predict which guarantee a given commit-before-or-after-processing pattern produces Explain what a real killed process proves that a diagram can&rsquo;t Connect delivery guarantees directly to Module 4&rsquo;s own offset-commit findings Three Guarantees, Defined Precisely At-most-once: each message is processed zero or one times. Never duplicated, but a crash at the wrong moment can lose one outright. At-least-once: each …
summary: Define at-most-once, at-least-once, and exactly-once precisely, then kill a real consumer process with SIGKILL to prove what each one actually costs -- a lost message under at-most-once, a duplicated one under at-least-once.
title: Lesson 1 - Delivery Guarantees

content:
Welcome to Window Functions GROUP BY (Module 2) answers &ldquo;what&rsquo;s the total per category?&rdquo; by collapsing every row in a category down to one. That&rsquo;s exactly wrong for a different kind of question: &ldquo;what&rsquo;s each product&rsquo;s rank within its category?&rdquo; — every row needs to stay, each one just needs to know something about the group it belongs to. That&rsquo;s what a window function does: it computes across a set of related rows without collapsing them.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Write a window function with OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...) Use ROW_NUMBER() to find the top N rows within each group Explain exactly how RANK() and DENSE_RANK() differ from ROW_NUMBER() and from each other Recognize a real tie in data and know which ranking function handles it the way you actually want This lesson&rsquo;s code was run against DuckDB 1.5.5, verified on 2026-08-12 — the version and date this whole course is pinned to. If …
summary: Rank rows within groups without collapsing them using ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and DENSE_RANK -- and see the real difference between them on a genuine tie.
title: Lesson 1 - Window Functions: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and Friends

content:
Welcome to Lists vs Arrays Every Thistlewood column you&rsquo;ve worked with so far holds one scalar value per row &ndash; a string, a number, a date. Polars also has two dtypes whose values are themselves collections: pl.List and pl.Array. They look similar in a printed table, but they enforce a different rule about row length, and this lesson verifies that rule directly rather than describing it from memory.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Explain the difference between pl.List (variable length per row) and pl.Array (fixed length per row) Reproduce the error Polars raises when you try to force rows of different lengths into a pl.Array Recognize which of Thistlewood&rsquo;s own columns is naturally list-shaped, and why Build a small, honestly-labeled illustrative pl.Array example for a genuinely fixed-length case A Real Variable-Length Column Thistlewood&rsquo;s order-line data is the natural example here: an order can have anywhere from 1 to 4 line items, so a column …
summary: The empirically-verified constraint that separates pl.List from pl.Array: pl.List tolerates a different length per row, pl.Array demands the same fixed length on every row and raises an error the moment that's not true.
title: Lesson 1 - Lists vs Arrays

content:
Welcome to Unit-Testing Tasks Every DAG so far in this course has been tested the same way: write it, save it to .airflow-local/dags/, wait for the scheduler to notice it, trigger a run, and poll until it finishes. That&rsquo;s the right way to test that a DAG works — dependencies, trigger rules, retries, all of it. It is a slow, heavy way to test whether one function&rsquo;s logic is correct, and CityFlow&rsquo;s validate_trips task has logic worth testing on its own: five checks that decide, for every single trip, whether it&rsquo;s clean or quarantined.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Pull a task&rsquo;s decision logic out into a plain, importable function with no Airflow dependency at all Write real assert-based unit tests covering a valid case, multiple invalid cases, and a genuine edge case Explain, with a real measured number, why testing logic in isolation is faster than testing it by triggering a DAG Pulling the Logic Out, Not Copying It …
summary: validate_trips's five real data-quality checks, pulled out into a plain importable function and unit-tested in total isolation -- no scheduler, no Airflow install -- with real assert-based tests and a real 33x speed comparison against a live DAG trigger.
title: Lesson 1 - Unit-Testing Tasks

content:
Welcome to ConfigMaps and Secrets Every pod Module 5 ran had its behavior fixed at build time — nginx:alpine serves the same welcome page no matter what, and CityFlow&rsquo;s own zone-lookup API always answered from the exact same 265-zone file baked into its image. That&rsquo;s fine for a demo, but it&rsquo;s a real limitation: a production service usually needs to behave differently across environments — a different feature flag, a different downstream URL, a different access token — without a new image for every variation. This lesson gives you the two Kubernetes objects that solve that: ConfigMaps for ordinary settings, and Secrets for anything you don&rsquo;t want sitting in plain text.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Externalize a real service&rsquo;s runtime behavior into a ConfigMap, with no change to its image. Explain, precisely, why kubectl get secret -o yaml shows base64 rather than the real value — and why that is not encryption. Avoid a real, easy-to-hit …
summary: Externalize a real service's config from its image with a ConfigMap, and see exactly why a Secret is different: base64, not encryption.
title: Lesson 1 - ConfigMaps and Secrets

content:
Welcome to How a Loop Knows to Quit This is the safety and cost module, and its blunt version is this: a loop that can&rsquo;t stop isn&rsquo;t a tool, it&rsquo;s a bill. Back in Module 1 you learned that every loop needs a place to stop; now you&rsquo;ll design that stop deliberately. This first lesson is about the exits — the specific conditions that make a loop end. Most people set at most one (they hope it finishes), and that&rsquo;s exactly how loops run past the point of usefulness, wasting money and doing things you didn&rsquo;t want. A well-engineered loop has several exits, and always includes a safety one.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Name the four ways a loop can exit: success, budget, error, and give-up Explain why a success exit alone isn&rsquo;t enough Design a loop with both a success exit and a safety exit Recognize the cost of a loop with no safety exit Let&rsquo;s look at the exits.
A Loop Needs Exits, Plural Think of a running loop as needing a set …

content:
Welcome to Schemas For five modules you have run queries — typed them at a live session, watched them execute, checked the answer against Course 1&rsquo;s verified ground truth. This module changes the frame. A production ETL is not something you run and watch; it is a job that wakes at 2 a.m., reads whatever the source dropped, and writes a result other systems depend on, with nobody there to eyeball the output. The very first thing that job needs — before it reads a single row — is to know the exact shape of the data it is about to process. That shape is the schema: the column names, their types, and whether each may be null. And the first discipline of production data engineering is that you declare the schema rather than asking Spark to guess it.
This lesson makes the case concretely, on CityFlow&rsquo;s taxi data, and it makes it by measurement. You&rsquo;ll build the taxi schema explicitly with StructType and StructField, read the CSV against it, and confirm every type with …
summary: Declare CityFlow's taxi schema with StructType instead of inferring it, and measure the cost of inference — a full extra pass that makes inferSchema=True 3.0x slower than an explicit read on the 200,000-row CSV, while parquet carries its own typed schema in the footer for free.
title: Lesson 1 - Schemas

content:
Welcome to Dicts &amp; Sets: O(1) Lookups &amp; Dedup Module 5 taught CityFlow&rsquo;s pipeline to use every core it has. A multiprocessing.Pool took a job that ground through six taxi partitions in 9.60 s on one core and finished it in 2.42 s across six — a real 3.96x, earned by putting idle hardware to work. That is a genuine win, and it is also the last easy one. You cannot buy a 20x by adding cores to a 10-core machine. The next multiple has to come from somewhere else: doing less work per trip in the first place. Ten cores running a wasteful loop is still a wasteful loop, just louder.
Here is where the waste is hiding. Every row in the trip table carries a PULocationID — an integer like 132. The dashboard does not show integers; it shows &ldquo;JFK Airport, Queens.&rdquo; So somewhere in the pipeline, every single trip has to turn a number into a name. That is a lookup, and January 2024 alone has 2,964,624 of them. Do that lookup against a list and each one is a scan — walk the …
summary: Replace a list scan with a dict on CityFlow's zone lookup and measure the difference on real NYC taxi data — 36.5x faster on isolated lookups, 19.2x faster enriching 2,964,624 real trips — then dedup the same month with a set in 0.52 s where a list-based check would take about 16 …
title: Lesson 1 - Dicts & Sets: O(1) Lookups & Dedup

content:
Welcome to The Autoregressive Idea You have built every mechanical part of a transformer: token and position embeddings, scaled dot-product attention, multi-head attention, and the full transformer block with residuals and layer norm. What you do not yet have is a reason for the model to compute anything, an objective that turns a stack of matrix multiplies into something that learns language. This module supplies that objective, and it is astonishingly simple: predict the next token.
That single idea, done at every position of a sequence and repeated over a corpus, is all that GPT is trained to do. In this first lesson you will not build any new model machinery. Instead you will set up the learning problem the rest of the module solves: how a language model assigns probability to text, how you turn a raw token sequence into supervised (input, target) pairs by shifting it, and why a transformer can make all of a sequence&rsquo;s next-token predictions at once, in parallel, where a …
summary: Frame language modeling as autoregressive next-token prediction, build shifted (input, target) pairs in NumPy, and compute the uniform-random loss baseline your GPT must beat.
title: Lesson 1 - The Autoregressive Idea

content:
Welcome to Why Agents Are Harder to Evaluate For five modules you have graded Docent — our Meridian documentation assistant — by looking at the answer it produced. Retrieval happened for it: some code fetched two doc pages, handed them to Claude, and Claude wrote a reply. There was exactly one model output per question, and evaluation meant asking one question of it: is that answer right?
This module changes the shape of the thing you are grading. A real assistant is often an agent: instead of being handed context, it decides for itself to search the docs, reads what comes back, maybe searches again, and only then answers. That autonomy is powerful, but it means the agent no longer produces a single output. It produces a trajectory — a sequence of tool calls and observations that leads to the final answer. And a trajectory can go wrong in far more places than a single answer can. This lesson makes that concrete by turning Docent into a tool-using agent, running it live, and printing …
summary: See why grading an agent means grading a whole trajectory of tool calls, not one answer, by running a tool-using Docent live and printing the path it takes to each answer.
title: Lesson 1 - Why Agents Are Harder to Evaluate

content:
Welcome to From ARIMA to SARIMA Module 5 (AR, MA, ARMA, ARIMA) ended on a precise, measured failure: a non-seasonal ARIMA could not beat a one-line seasonal baseline on Cyclepath, because it had no term for seasonality. The diagnosis pointed straight at the cure: give the model an explicit seasonal mechanism. That is SARIMA, which stands for Seasonal ARIMA. It does not replace anything you learned. It repeats the ARIMA machinery at the seasonal lag, so the model can say &ldquo;this month depends on its recent neighbors and on the same month a year ago&rdquo;.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Read the full SARIMA(p,d,q)(P,D,Q)[s] notation Explain what the seasonal period s is and how to choose it Map each seasonal order (P, D, Q) to its non-seasonal twin (p, d, q) Explain why the seasonal terms are the mechanism ARIMA lacked Let&rsquo;s read the notation.
The SARIMA Notation A SARIMA model is written with two sets of orders:
SARIMA(p, d, q)(P, D, Q)[s] …
summary: SARIMA extends ARIMA with a second set of orders — (P, D, Q) at the seasonal lag s — that mirror the non-seasonal (p, d, q) but operate a full cycle apart. Meet the SARIMA(p,d,q)(P,D,Q)[s] notation and why each seasonal term exists.
title: Lesson 1 - From ARIMA to SARIMA

content:
Welcome to Peeking and Optional Stopping Here&rsquo;s a habit that feels responsible and is quietly disastrous: you launch an experiment, and because you&rsquo;re eager (and the dashboard is right there), you check it every day. The moment it crosses p &lt; 0.05, you stop and declare a winner. What could be wrong with stopping as soon as you have significance? Everything. That single, intuitive behavior — peeking and optional stopping — is probably the most common way careful teams ship false positives, and it doesn&rsquo;t announce itself: every individual p-value is computed correctly. In this lesson you&rsquo;ll watch it inflate your error rate almost four-fold, on data where there&rsquo;s nothing to find at all.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Explain why repeatedly testing and stopping early inflates the false-positive rate Quantify the inflation with a simulation of null experiments Distinguish a fixed-horizon analysis from optional stopping Name the correct …
summary: Watching a test and stopping the moment it hits significance feels efficient — but it quietly turns your 5% false-positive rate into nearly 20%. See the inflation happen in simulation, and learn the fixes.
title: Lesson 1 - Peeking and Optional Stopping

content:
Welcome to Why Agents Need Retrieval Your agent is capable now — it loops, calls tools, remembers, and plans. But ask it something that depends on your data — &ldquo;what&rsquo;s our refund policy?&rdquo;, &ldquo;what did the Q3 report say?&rdquo;, &ldquo;is the Arashiyama bamboo grove worth an early start?&rdquo; — and it does one of two things: answers from whatever happened to be in its training data, or makes something up that sounds right. Neither is good enough for a real product. The model&rsquo;s knowledge is frozen at training time and blind to anything private. This module gives the agent a way out: retrieval — looking facts up in a knowledge base you control, and answering from what it finds. This lesson is about why that matters before we build it.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Explain the three things a model&rsquo;s built-in knowledge can&rsquo;t do: be current, be private, be certain Describe retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and the …
summary: A model only knows its training data — so it can't see your documents or today's facts, and it guesses when it doesn't know. See why retrieval fixes this and meet the retrieve-augment-generate pattern.
title: Lesson 1 - Why Agents Need Retrieval

content:
Welcome to Branching Strategies You already know how to make a branch. This lesson is about the bigger question a team has to answer: which branches should exist, and how does work flow into the line everyone ships from? That agreement is called a branching strategy, and choosing one is one of the first decisions a team makes — because without a shared convention, everyone invents their own, and the repository turns into a maze. The good news is that the industry has converged on a handful of well-understood strategies. Learn the three main ones and you&rsquo;ll recognize almost any team&rsquo;s setup on sight.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Explain what a branching strategy is and why a team needs one Describe GitHub Flow, Git Flow, and trunk-based development Compare their trade-offs in complexity and release cadence Choose a strategy that fits a given team and project This builds on branches (Module 3) and pull requests (Module 5). Let&rsquo;s begin.

content:
Welcome to Querying SQLite from Python So far you have written SQL inside a database tool and read the results in a table. In this lesson you bring SQL into Python. You will connect to a real database file, run a query from your own code, and get the results back as Python objects you can loop over, slice, and pass to other functions.
The tool that makes this possible is sqlite3, a library that comes built into Python — there is nothing to install. SQLite is a database that needs no separate server; it stores an entire database in a single file on disk. That makes SQLite ideal for datasets that are too large to comfortably hold in memory but small enough to fit on disk, and it makes databases easy to share: you can hand someone a single .db file.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Connect to a SQLite database from Python with sqlite3.connect() Create a cursor and run SQL queries with execute() Fetch results as a list of tuples and read individual values out of them …
summary: Connect to a SQLite database from Python and execute queries using cursors and tuples.
title: Lesson 1 - Running SQL Queries with sqlite3

content:
Welcome to Security First Steps Your Task Manager has a glaring problem: anyone can do anything. There&rsquo;s no sign-in, no notion of who is calling — so there&rsquo;s no way to keep one person&rsquo;s tasks separate from another&rsquo;s, or to stop a stranger from deleting everything. The fix is authentication: a way for a client to prove who it is. FastAPI has first-class support for the OAuth2 password flow, the standard &ldquo;log in with a username and password, then carry a token&rdquo; pattern used by APIs everywhere. This lesson sets up the skeleton of that flow; the next lessons make it secure with hashing and real tokens.
By the end you&rsquo;ll have a working login endpoint and a protected route — the foundation everything else in this module builds on.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Describe the OAuth2 password flow at a high level Build a /token login endpoint with OAuth2PasswordRequestForm Protect an endpoint by requiring a token with …
summary: Take your first security steps in FastAPI: the OAuth2 password flow, a login endpoint with OAuth2PasswordRequestForm, and protecting a route with OAuth2PasswordBearer.
title: Lesson 1 - Security First Steps

content:
Welcome to Why Vector Databases In Module 5 you built a working semantic search engine: embed every document, embed the query, compare the query to all of them, and return the closest. For fifteen FAQs that is instant and perfectly fine. But that approach hides a cost that grows with your data — every query re-scans every vector, and you have to keep all those vectors in memory and re-embed them whenever your program restarts. A vector database removes all three problems. It stores your embeddings on disk, builds an index so search doesn&rsquo;t touch every vector, and lets you attach and filter on metadata.
This lesson is about why that matters. The next lessons get hands-on with Chroma.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Explain why brute-force search doesn&rsquo;t scale Describe what a vector database stores and indexes Explain what an approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) index buys you Describe the &ldquo;store once, query many&rdquo; pattern and metadata filtering …
summary: See why the brute-force search from Module 5 breaks down at scale, and what a vector database — with its index and metadata — does to fix it.
title: Lesson 1 - Why Vector Databases

content:
Welcome to Setting Limits The last lesson said every loop needs a safety exit. This lesson makes the most important one concrete: the budget. A budget is a limit you set before the loop runs, so it physically can&rsquo;t cost more than you decided the task was worth. There are three kinds — turns, time, and money — and knowing which to set, and to what, is what keeps a loop bounded. This matters most once an agent runs the loop for you: by hand, your own patience is an accidental budget, but an automated loop will happily spend until something explicit stops it.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Set a budget in the three units that matter: turns, time, and money Choose which budget matters for a given loop Size a budget to what the task is actually worth Explain why the money cap is the critical one for automated loops Let&rsquo;s look at the three budgets.
Three Budgets, Set in Advance A budget answers &ldquo;what&rsquo;s the most this loop is allowed to consume before …
summary: Set a loop's budget before you run it — in turns, time, and money — so it can never quietly cost more than the task is worth.
title: Lesson 2 - Setting Limits: Loop Budgets

content:
Welcome to Read → Clean → Transform Lesson 1 gave you the first discipline of a production job: declare the schema, never infer it, so the read is a contract rather than a guess. You now have a StructType that describes every taxi column exactly. This lesson builds the body of the job that sits on top of that contract — the part that turns three raw Parquet files into CityFlow&rsquo;s zone-hour analytics table — and it makes one architectural decision that every maintainable pipeline shares: the body is a few small functions, not one long chain of DataFrame calls.
That choice sounds like style, but it is the difference between a job you can trust at 3 a.m. and one you can only pray over. A single 40-line .filter().withColumn().join().groupBy() chain runs fine right up until the day a number looks wrong, and then you have nowhere to stand — no seam to inspect, no piece to test, no way to ask &ldquo;is the cleaning wrong or the aggregation wrong?&rdquo; without re-reading the whole …
summary: Build the ETL body as three tested functions — read_trips, clean_trips, transform_to_report — on the real taxi quarter, and unit-test the cleaner on a four-row frame that proves it drops the 2002 stray, keeps both halves of a reversal pair, and cancels them to leave $40.00.
title: Lesson 2 - Read → Clean → Transform

content:
Welcome to Stacks &amp; Queues CityFlow&rsquo;s pipeline can now read a month of trips without drowning in memory (Module 4) and grind through them on every core at once (Module 5). But look closely at what those two modules never actually built: a place to put work. Module 4&rsquo;s loop read a batch and immediately processed it. Module 5&rsquo;s Pool was handed a finished list of six tasks before it started. Neither had to cope with the situation every real streaming pipeline lives in — batches arriving while earlier ones are still being processed, piling up somewhere, waiting their turn. That waiting area has a name. It&rsquo;s a queue, and the order it hands work back out is not a detail; it is the whole design.
Two orders matter. FIFO (first in, first out) is what you want when work must be handled fairly in arrival order — the batch that showed up first gets processed first, and nothing starves while newer arrivals jump ahead. LIFO (last in, first out) is what you want when you …
summary: Give CityFlow's streaming pipeline somewhere to hold work that has arrived but isn't processed yet, and learn why the obvious choice is a trap: draining a 200,000-element queue takes 3,012.6 ms with list.pop(0) but 3.6 ms with collections.deque.popleft() - a measured 829x gap.
title: Lesson 2 - Stacks & Queues

content:
Welcome to The Causal Mask In the previous lesson you framed language modeling as an autoregressive task: at every position the model predicts the next token from the tokens that came before it. That objective has a strict rule hidden inside it. When your mini-GPT is asked to predict the character at position t+1 t+1 , it is only allowed to look at positions 0 0 through t t . The self-attention head you built in Module 2 breaks that rule flagrantly: it lets every position attend to every position, future included. Position t t would get to see position t+1 t+1 — the very answer it is supposed to predict.
This lesson fixes that with one small, precise change: the causal mask. You set the attention scores for future positions to negative infinity before the softmax, so those positions get essentially zero weight and each query attends only to itself and the past. The result is a lower-triangular attention matrix, and it is the single mechanism that turns a generic attention block into a …
summary: Implement the causal mask that makes self-attention autoregressive: set future scores to negative infinity before softmax so each position attends only to itself and the past, then verify the backward pass zeros the masked gradients.
title: Lesson 2 - The Causal Mask

content:
Welcome to Task Success &amp; Outcome Metrics In Lesson 1 you watched a single answer unfold into a whole path: the agentic Docent &ndash; our assistant for the Meridian serverless database docs &ndash; decides for itself to call search_docs, reads what comes back, and only then answers. That path is rich to inspect, and the next two lessons dig into it. But before we grade how the agent worked, we have to answer the blunt question a user actually cares about: did it get the job done? For Docent, &ldquo;the job&rdquo; is a correct, grounded answer to a docs question &ndash; and, just as importantly, a clean refusal when the docs can&rsquo;t answer at all.
This lesson is about the outcome side of agent evaluation and its headline metric, task success rate: the fraction of tasks the agent completed correctly. It sounds simple, and that simplicity is exactly why it&rsquo;s the first number anyone looks at. The catch is that &ldquo;correctly&rdquo; has to be made checkable: every task …
summary: Measure the headline agent metric -- task success rate -- by running the agentic Docent over a golden task set, defining a per-task verifier, and watching a broken-retriever regression drop success from 8/8 to 1/8.
title: Lesson 2 - Task Success & Outcome Metrics

content:
Welcome to Seasonal AR and MA Terms Lesson 1 said the seasonal orders mirror the non-seasonal ones at the seasonal lag. This lesson makes that concrete. A seasonal AR(1) term does for the seasonal lag exactly what a non-seasonal AR(1) does for lag 1: it says today&rsquo;s value is a fraction of a value a fixed distance back — except the distance is a full season (12 months) instead of one step. Once you see a seasonal AR term recover a known coefficient and produce its distinctive autocorrelation fingerprint, the seasonal MA term and seasonal differencing fall into place by analogy.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Write the seasonal AR(1) relationship and explain what its coefficient means Recover a known seasonal AR coefficient from synthetic data Recognize the seasonal AR fingerprint: ACF spikes at multiples of the season length Explain seasonal MA and seasonal differencing by analogy to their non-seasonal twins Let&rsquo;s build a seasonal AR process.
The Seasonal …
summary: A seasonal AR term relates each value to the same point one cycle earlier — this July to last July. Build a pure seasonal AR(1) process, recover its known coefficient of 0.6, and see its ACF spike at every multiple of the season length.
title: Lesson 2 - Seasonal AR and MA Terms

content:
Welcome to Multiple Comparisons In the last lesson, looking at one test many times inflated your false-positive rate. This lesson is the same disease from a different source: looking at many tests once. You launch an experiment and, because you have a dashboard full of numbers, you check the click rate, the signup rate, revenue, retention, time on page, and fifteen more — and the moment any one of them crosses p &lt; 0.05, you declare a win. Every individual test is computed correctly at α = 0.05, just like before. But asking twenty questions and celebrating the one that answered &ldquo;yes&rdquo; is not the same as asking one question, and the gap between them is enormous. On data with no real effect at all, twenty metrics give you a coin-flip&rsquo;s-worth of chances to fool yourself.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Explain why testing many metrics, variants, or segments inflates the false-positive rate Compute the family-wise error rate with the formula 1 - (1 - α)^m …
summary: Test 20 metrics at once and there's a 64% chance one comes back a false 'winner' — see the inflation in simulation, and correct it with Bonferroni and its more powerful cousins.

content:
Welcome to Building a Knowledge Base In Lesson 1 you saw why an agent needs retrieval, and that the knowledge base is really the memory module&rsquo;s machinery pointed at documents. Now you build it. The job is small once you name it: take a document, cut it into bite-sized passages, turn each passage into a vector with the same embed() you used for long-term memory, and store the lot. To retrieve, embed the user&rsquo;s question and return the passages whose vectors point most nearly the same way. That&rsquo;s a knowledge base — chunk, embed, index, search — and by the end of this lesson you&rsquo;ll have one that answers questions about a pair of travel guides.
The shape is deliberately familiar. In Module 4 you wrote a VectorMemory with add(note) and search(query, k); here you write a KnowledgeBase with add_document(source, text) and search(query, k). The only genuinely new piece is chunking — a document is too big to embed as one blob, so you split it into passages first. …
summary: Chunk documents into passages, embed each one, and search by similarity to build the store your agent retrieves from.
title: Lesson 2 - Building a Knowledge Base

content:
Welcome to Commit Conventions and Great Messages You make commits all the time, but how much thought goes into the message? It&rsquo;s tempting to type fixed stuff and move on. The problem shows up months later, when you (or a teammate) open git log to understand why a line of code exists — and find a wall of vague, inconsistent messages that explain nothing. A commit message is the one chance you get to leave a note for the future. Done well, your history becomes living documentation; done badly, it becomes noise everyone learns to ignore. This lesson teaches you to write messages a team can rely on, anchored on a widely used format called Conventional Commits.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Explain why commit history is documentation and what a good subject line communicates Write a great message with an imperative subject, a blank line, and a body that explains the why Apply the Conventional Commits format: type(scope): description, with breaking-change markers …
summary: Write commit messages a team can rely on using Conventional Commits — a clear type, scope, and imperative subject, plus a body that explains the why.
title: Lesson 2 - Commit Conventions and Great Messages

content:
Welcome to SQL Results in pandas In the last lesson you queried a SQLite database and got back a list of tuples. That works, but tuples make for clumsy analysis — there are no column names, and every calculation means looping and indexing by position. In this lesson you fix that by routing your query results straight into a pandas DataFrame, the table-shaped data structure at the heart of data analysis in Python.
A DataFrame gives you named columns, vectorized operations, and one-line plotting. Once your SQL results land in a DataFrame, the full power of pandas — filtering, grouping, sorting, charting — is available to you. SQLite is excellent at storing and querying data, but it cannot draw a chart; pandas and matplotlib can, so the natural move is to query in SQL and analyze in Python.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

Welcome to Getting Started with Chroma In Lesson 1 you saw why a vector database exists: it stores embeddings, documents, and metadata together, indexes them for fast search, and lets you embed once and query many times. Now you&rsquo;ll use one. Chroma is an open-source vector database that runs entirely on your own machine — no server to host, no account to create, no API key to manage. Even better, Chroma can do the embedding for you. In Module 5 you called an embedding model by hand and stored the vectors yourself; here you simply hand Chroma your text, and it embeds and stores it in a single call.
This lesson gets you from a blank file to a working semantic search in a handful of lines.

Welcome to Password Hashing and the Current User In Lesson 1 you built the skeleton of the OAuth2 password flow, but two big holes are still wide open. First, the login endpoint never actually checked the password — anyone could log in as anyone. Second, even if you stored passwords, storing them as plain text would be a catastrophe: one leaked database and every account is compromised. This lesson closes both holes. You&rsquo;ll learn to hash passwords so the real password is never written down anywhere, verify a submitted password at login, and write a get_current_user dependency that turns a token back into the user who&rsquo;s calling — rejecting anything invalid with a 401.
We&rsquo;ll keep the token simple for now (it&rsquo;s still basically the username), so we can focus on hashing and the current-user pattern. Real signed JWTs arrive in Lesson 3.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Explain why passwords must be hashed and never stored or logged in plain text Hash …
summary: Never store plain-text passwords: hash them with bcrypt, verify at login, and write a get_current_user dependency that turns a token into the logged-in user.
title: Lesson 2 - Password Hashing and the Current User

A batch task — an ETL run, a nightly report, exactly the kind of thing Module 3&rsquo;s cityflow-etl-job did as a bare docker run — is the opposite shape of problem. content:
Welcome to When a Loop Gets Stuck Not every failing loop runs away loudly. Some get quietly stuck — busy, active, producing new output every round, but never actually getting closer to done. This is more insidious than a runaway, because it looks like progress: the loop is clearly working. This lesson teaches you to recognize the three shapes a stuck loop takes, how to detect one early, and — most usefully — the root cause hiding behind almost all of them.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Recognize the three stuck patterns: oscillating, undoing its own work, and drifting Detect a stuck loop by watching for progress, not activity Trace a stuck loop back to its usual root cause Know what to do when you spot one Let&rsquo;s name the patterns.
Three Ways a Loop Gets Stuck A healthy loop converges: each round, the result gets measurably closer to done. A stuck loop is busy but not converging — the output keeps changing without improving. It happens in three recognizable …
summary: Some loops don't run away loudly — they get quietly stuck. Learn to spot oscillation, undoing its own work, and goal drift, and to find the root cause.
title: Lesson 3 - When a Loop Gets Stuck

But so far that result has only ever lived in memory. A production ETL is not a query you watch return; it is a job that writes something other systems read tomorrow morning. This lesson is the write, and it is not the throwaway .save() it looks like. How you lay the output down decides how fast every downstream query runs, how many files pile up, and whether a re-run corrupts the table or replaces it cleanly.

Welcome to Heaps &amp; Priority Queues CityFlow&rsquo;s dashboard opens with a single panel: the 10 busiest pickup zones this month. You already have everything you need to build it. Lesson 1 gave you a dict that maps a LocationID to a zone name in O(1), and Module 4 taught you to stream a month of trips through iter_batches without ever holding it in memory. Counting trips per zone is a Counter and one pass. Then comes the last step, and almost everyone writes the same line: sort the counts and take the first ten. It works. It is also the moment worth stopping on, because you just asked Python to put all 260 zones into perfect order — to decide whether the 187th busiest zone outranks the 188th — in order to answer a question that never asked about either of them. You did O(n log n) work to report ten rows.
There is a data structure whose entire purpose is that mismatch. A heap keeps one element — the smallest — instantly available and deliberately leaves everything else only roughly …

Welcome to The Decoder-Only Stack You have built every component a GPT needs. In Module 4 you turned token ids into vectors with token and position embeddings. In Module 5 you assembled the pre-norm transformer block. In the last two lessons of this module you made attention causal, so a position can only look at itself and the past. This lesson is the moment those parts stop being separate exercises and become a single model. You will assemble the decoder-only stack, the exact architecture that GPT uses, and write its forward pass end to end in NumPy.
The shape of the whole model is short enough to say in one breath: embed the token ids, run them through a stack of causal transformer blocks, normalize once at the end, and project to the vocabulary. That last projection produces, for every position in the sequence, a score for every possible next character. Those scores are the model&rsquo;s next-token predictions. This lesson is forward-only, using random untrained weights; the loss …

Welcome to Tool-Call Correctness In Lesson 2 you asked whether agentic Docent &ndash; our assistant for the Meridian serverless database docs &ndash; accomplished the task. But task success is an outcome metric: it grades the destination and stays silent about the journey. An agent can reach the right answer through a call it should never have made, and it can produce a wrong answer because of a single bad tool call buried three steps back. This lesson zooms all the way in on those calls. We stop looking at the final answer entirely and evaluate the tool calls themselves &ndash; one layer of the trajectory, scored on its own terms.
Three questions define a correct tool call, and they are genuinely different questions. First, tool selection: did Docent call the right tool for the job &ndash; and just as important, did it call the tool at all when it should have, rather than answering a docs question from the model&rsquo;s parametric memory? Second, argument validity: were the arguments …

content:
Welcome to Simpson&rsquo;s Paradox Here&rsquo;s a result that looks impossible. You segment your experiment by user type, and the control arm converts better among new users and better among returning users — it wins in every subgroup you look at. Then you check the overall number and the treatment is ahead. Not tied — clearly ahead. Every subgroup says control, the aggregate says treatment, and both are computed from the exact same data with the exact same arithmetic. This is Simpson&rsquo;s paradox, and it isn&rsquo;t a rounding glitch or a bug in your code. It&rsquo;s a real feature of how weighted averages combine, and in an A/B test it&rsquo;s usually trying to tell you something important.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Recognize Simpson&rsquo;s paradox: a treatment that loses in every subgroup yet wins overall Explain the mechanism — an imbalanced segment mix between arms Understand why the paradox should not appear under clean randomization Use the paradox as a …
summary: A treatment can lose in every single subgroup yet win overall — see how an imbalanced segment mix flips the comparison, and why that flip is a red flag in a randomized experiment.
title: Lesson 3 - Simpson's Paradox

Welcome to Retrieval as a Tool In Lesson 2 you built a knowledge base: chunk documents into passages, embed them, and search them by similarity. Now you have to decide when the agent retrieves. There are two ways, and the difference matters. The first is to always retrieve before answering — every question runs through search first, then the model answers from whatever came back. That&rsquo;s a fixed pipeline, and it&rsquo;s exactly what you&rsquo;ll build in Lesson 4. The second is to hand the agent a search_knowledge tool and let it decide, mid-loop, whether and when to look something up. That&rsquo;s agentic RAG, and it&rsquo;s what this lesson is about.
The shift is small in code but large in capability. When retrieval is a tool, it becomes just another action in the agent loop you already wrote — the model can skip it, call it once, or call it several times with refined queries, all on its own judgment. This lesson builds the tool, plugs it into the canonical run_agent loop, and …

title: Lesson 3 - Retrieval as a Tool

Welcome to Working Together Without Stepping on Toes Back in Module 3 you met the merge conflict — that moment when Git can&rsquo;t decide whose change wins and hands the decision back to you. It felt dramatic the first time. But on a team, conflicts aren&rsquo;t a special event; they&rsquo;re a routine part of many people editing one shared codebase. The teams that suffer aren&rsquo;t the ones that have conflicts — everyone has them — they&rsquo;re the ones whose conflicts are huge, tangled, and rare enough to be terrifying. This lesson is about the everyday habits that keep conflicts small, frequent, and boring. None of them are new Git commands so much as new rhythms: how often you integrate, how big you let your work grow, and how clearly you coordinate with the people around you.

content:
Welcome to JWT Access Tokens In Lesson 2 you turned a token into the current user — but the token itself was still flimsy. It was just the username with -token glued on, so anyone could forge one for any account by typing a name, and it never expired. A real access token has to be tamper-proof (the server can tell if someone edited it) and time-limited (it stops working after a while). The standard tool for both jobs is the JSON Web Token, or JWT.
In this lesson you&rsquo;ll replace the placeholder with a genuine signed JWT. You&rsquo;ll encode the username and an expiry into it, hand it out at login, and verify it on every protected request — letting the library reject forged or stale tokens for you.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

summary: Issue real, signed access tokens with JWT: encode claims like the user and an expiry, verify and decode them, and reject tampered or expired tokens automatically.
title: Lesson 3 - JWT Access Tokens

Welcome to Metadata and Filtering In the previous lesson you stored a handful of documents in Chroma and searched them by meaning alone. That works well when every document is fair game, but real systems are rarely that simple. You usually want to search within a category: only shipping articles, only documents written this year, only items tagged for a particular product line. Semantic similarity finds the closest text; metadata filtering decides which text is even allowed to compete. This lesson shows you how to attach that structured information and use it, and then how to save the whole database to disk so you never have to rebuild it from scratch.

Welcome to Teaching a Loop to Ask So far the exits you&rsquo;ve designed end the loop: success, budget, error, give-up. This lesson adds a different kind of exit — one that pauses the loop so it can ask you a question, then continues with your answer. This is escalation, and it&rsquo;s one of the most valuable things you can build into a hands-off loop. A loop that knows when to stop and ask, rather than confidently guessing, is the difference between an agent you can trust with real work and one that will occasionally do something irreversible and wrong at full speed.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Explain what escalation is and why it beats guessing Recognize the three triggers that should make a loop ask Write escalation rules into a loop&rsquo;s brief Reframe &ldquo;asking&rdquo; as the loop being honest, not failing Let&rsquo;s start with why a loop should ever ask.
Asking Beats Guessing An autonomous loop is always making decisions — what to do next, how to …

Welcome to Idempotent Jobs Lesson 3 gave CityFlow a partitioned analytics table: the zone-hour report written out as Parquet, clustered by month, so a dashboard query for February reads February&rsquo;s files and skips the rest. That table is the thing the scheduler will rebuild every night. Which surfaces the question this whole module has been building toward — the one that separates a demo from a job you can actually leave running. What happens when the job runs twice? Not hypothetically: a task fails and Spark retries it, a schedule fires twice because someone re-enabled it, an on-call engineer re-runs last night&rsquo;s backfill by hand to be safe. A job that produces the right answer once and the wrong answer on the retry is not a job you can trust to run unattended, and unattended is the entire point.
This is the same problem Course 1 solved in its capstone with a SQLite warehouse: a primary key on (zone, hour) and INSERT OR REPLACE, so loading the same batch twice replaced rows …

Welcome to Choosing the Right Structure Three lessons in, CityFlow&rsquo;s toolbox is full. Lesson 1 showed that hashing makes a dict find a zone by id in constant time while a list hunts for it, and that a set answers &ldquo;have I seen this trip?&rdquo; the same way. Lesson 2 showed that a deque gives a streaming buffer a genuinely cheap front, where list.pop(0) quietly re-copies every element behind it. Lesson 3 showed that a heap hands you the ten busiest zones without ever sorting the other two hundred and fifty-five. Four structures, four convincing demos — and one problem: knowing what each one does is not the same as knowing which one to reach for on a Tuesday afternoon when the dashboard is slow and a teammate asks whether the zone join should be indexed.
That is the gap this lesson closes, and it closes it by replacing the wrong question with the right one. The wrong question is &ldquo;which structure is fastest?&rdquo; — it has no answer, because a structure that is slow to …

content:
Welcome to The Language-Modeling Head &amp; Loss In the last three lessons you built the body of a GPT: token and position embeddings feed a stack of causal transformer blocks, and out comes a tensor of hidden states shaped (B, T, C), one C-dimensional vector summarizing what the model knows at each position. That tensor is rich, but it is not yet an answer. A language model has exactly one job: at every position, predict the next token. This lesson adds the two pieces that turn hidden states into that prediction and, crucially, into a single number you can train against.
The first piece is the language-modeling head, a plain linear layer that projects each hidden vector to one score per vocabulary token. The second is the loss: softmax those scores into a probability distribution over the vocabulary, and measure how much probability the model put on the token that actually came next. Averaged over every position in the batch, that is the softmax cross-entropy next-token loss, the …
summary: Project the transformer's hidden states to vocabulary logits with the LM head, then turn them into a trainable softmax cross-entropy next-token loss in pure NumPy, gradient-checked.

Welcome to Trajectory Evaluation In Lesson 2 you asked whether Docent &ndash; our agent for the Meridian serverless database docs &ndash; accomplished the task, and in Lesson 3 you asked whether each individual tool call was correct: the right tool, valid arguments, a sensible query. Both are essential, and both share a blind spot. They look at the endpoints &ndash; the final answer, or one call at a time &ndash; and never at the shape of the whole run.
Here&rsquo;s the problem that shape hides. Ask two versions of Docent the same question and both come back with &ldquo;HTTP 429.&rdquo; One of them searched the docs once and answered. The other searched, ignored what came back, searched again with a barely-different query, searched a third time, and only then answered. Same outcome. Every individual tool call was a valid search_docs call with reasonable arguments, so a per-call check passes each one. Yet the second agent burned three times the calls, latency, and tokens, and wandered …

Welcome to Diagnostics: Is the Model Adequate? Lesson 3&rsquo;s forecast looked great. It tracked the seasonal curve almost exactly. But &ldquo;looks right on the test set&rdquo; is not proof a model is sound. It could be fitting this particular year well by luck while leaving real structure unexplained. Diagnostics answer the harder question: are the model&rsquo;s residuals white noise? A residual is the gap between what the model predicted and what actually happened. If the residuals still contain a pattern, the model missed something, no matter how good one forecast looks. This is the exact check Module 4&rsquo;s (Autocorrelation: ACF and PACF) preview model failed, and this lesson shows the finished model passing it.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
State what a residual diagnostic is checking: are the residuals white noise? Run and interpret the Ljung-Box test for leftover autocorrelation Read the summary&rsquo;s built-in normality and heteroskedasticity checks …
summary: A good-looking forecast isn't proof. Run the Ljung-Box test on the SARIMA's residuals — it passes at p = 0.209 where Module 4's preview model failed at p = 0.000 — plus normality and variance checks, to confirm the model is genuinely adequate.
title: Lesson 4 - Diagnostics: Is the Model Adequate?

Welcome to Sanity Checks and Threats to Validity Every lesson so far has assumed the experiment ran correctly and you just had to analyze it well. Reality is messier: assignment code has bugs, events get dropped, and users react to change itself in ways that have nothing to do with whether your change is good. Before you trust any number an experiment produces, you run a handful of cheap sanity checks that catch a broken pipeline — and you stay alert to a set of threats to validity that can invalidate a result even when every statistic is computed perfectly. The mindset is simple: an experiment&rsquo;s number is only as trustworthy as the plumbing behind it, and these checks are how you inspect the plumbing before you ship a decision.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Run a sample ratio mismatch (SRM) check with a chi-squared goodness-of-fit test Recognize an SRM failure as a &ldquo;stop and fix&rdquo; signal, not something to analyze around Name the main threats to …

Welcome to Tags and Releases Your team has merged a batch of work into main, run the tests, and decided it&rsquo;s ready for the world. How do you mark this exact commit as the version you shipped, so you can point a teammate, a customer, or your future self straight back to it? Commit hashes like d638b86 are precise but meaningless to humans. What you want is a name — v1.0.0 — that says &ldquo;this is the version we released.&rdquo; That name is called a tag, and a tag dressed up with notes and downloads is a release. Welcome to Protecting Routes and Scopes In Lesson 3 you built get_current_user: a dependency that decodes a signed JWT and hands you the user making the request. That answers one question — who are you? This lesson answers the next one — what are you allowed to do? The two are not the same. A logged-in user has proven their identity, but that doesn&rsquo;t mean they should be able to delete other people&rsquo;s data or reach an admin-only endpoint. The first question is authentication; the second is authorization, and a production API needs both.
The good news: you already have the tools. Authorization in FastAPI is just more dependency injection. You protect a route by depending on the current user, and you add a permission check by writing a small dependency that builds on get_current_user and refuses the request when the rules aren&rsquo;t met. Along the way you&rsquo;ll see exactly why a missing token gives a 401 while a logged-in-but-not-allowed user gives a 403 — a distinction …
